# Checks that came out safe

3199 checks after cycle 39. Each entry gives what was tested, why it is safe, and the evidence.

## Arbitrum Nitro and Orbit chains

- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, cycle 1. A1: whether an unlock flag, a currency delta or a synced currency can survive from one transaction into another through Nitro's extra transaction types (deposits, internal transactions, retryable submission, auto-redeems, manual redeems). Result: The state transition runs the ArbOS start hook and then StateDB.Prepare, which replaces the transient storage map, before any contract code runs. Deposit, internal and submit-retryable transactions end inside the hook and execute no contract code. Each scheduled redeem is appended to a queue and applied as its own transaction. Lock.sol:10-27, CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41, CurrencyReserves.sol:15-38 and NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:12-34 therefore see one transaction as on Ethereum. The go-ethereum file was read on the fork's master branch, which may differ from the commit pinned by the release. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/master/core/state_transition.go and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/arbos/block_processor.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 1. A3 and A4: whether any ArbOS precompile can serve as an ERC-20 face of the native asset or as a currency whose transfer succeeds without moving anything. Result: balanceOf(address) and transfer(address,uint256) revert on every precompile address from 0x64 to 0x74 and on 0xff when called from the PoolManager address. sync calls balanceOf (PoolManager.sol:285, Currency.sol:94) and reverts, so no delta can ever be credited in such a currency, and a take reverts in Currency.sol:64-86. ArbInfo.getBalance exposes native balances under a different selector that the PoolManager never calls. Evidence: eth_call on https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc, https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com and https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, cycle 1. A3: native balance credited to the PoolManager without a call, through a deposit transaction or a retryable refund address chosen by a parent chain sender. Result: Native settlement credits msg.value only (PoolManager.sol:353-354) and sync of the native currency records no balance (PoolManager.sol:281-283). A forced credit raises address(this).balance and is credited to nobody. It cannot be claimed and it cannot make a settle revert. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/arbos/tx_processor.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, cycle 1. Whether a parent chain message can debit the PoolManager's native balance by making the PoolManager the aliased sender of an unsigned transaction or retryable. Result: The child chain sender is the parent chain msg.sender plus a fixed offset. Producing the PoolManager address needs control of one specific 160-bit parent chain address, which is a preimage search. Signed messages use the signer instead. No other transaction type takes fees from an account other than its sender. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/arbos/parse_l2.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, cycle 1. A12: who can produce a call from the owner 0x2BAD8182C09F50c8318d769245beA52C32Be46CD, and what the owner and fee controller can do to pool funds. Result: The address has no code on either chain and equals the Ethereum timelock 0x1a9C8182C09F50C8318d769245beA52c32BE35BC plus the alias offset. Both chains settle to Ethereum, so only that timelock, through each chain's inbox, yields this sender. The owner can only set the fee controller (ProtocolFees.sol:29-32). The controller can set a fee of at most 1000 pips per direction (ProtocolFees.sol:35-41, ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8, 25-32) and withdraw at most protocolFeesAccrued (ProtocolFees.sol:54-56). Evidence: https://docs.arbitrum.io/how-arbitrum-works/deep-dives/l1-to-l2-messaging
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, cycle 1. Permissionless collect on the fee controller contracts 0x6b3c04567cc62fc5d6ab8d50f1bc1dee161eb2cc and 0x6d0009504d129cf5002dba61d9ae8575aa79314c, including a call made inside an unlock. Result: An eth_call of collect from an arbitrary sender succeeds on Arbitrum One, so anyone can trigger collectProtocolFees. The amount is capped by a checked subtraction from protocolFeesAccrued (ProtocolFees.sol:54-55), the transfer goes to the controller's fixed TOKEN_JAR, and a synced ERC-20 currency is refused (ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). A collection can only lower the PoolManager balance by fees that were already set aside, so it cannot create a settle credit. The Robinhood controller has the same code length and selectors. I did not simulate collect there. Evidence: https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc eth_call collect((address,uint256)[]) from 0x00000000000000000000000000000000000a11ce, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 1. A9: whether gas caps on these chains can make a large swap or a liquidity removal impossible to include. Result: All three chains report a per-transaction limit and a block limit of 32,000,000 execution gas, and the last transaction of a block may overshoot the block limit. Parent chain data cost is charged on top of execution gas. A removal touches two ticks (Pool.sol:146-238) and a swap loop costs gas per initialized tick crossed (Pool.sol:344-437), so both fit with a wide margin, and a swap can be split with a price limit. Evidence: eth_call ArbGasInfo.getGasAccountingParams() and getMaxTxGasLimit() on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22; https://docs.arbitrum.io/run-a-node/arbos-releases/arbos51
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 1. A2 and A3: the ArbOS native mint and burn precompile as a way for the chain to change the PoolManager's native balance or inflate the gas token. Result: mintNativeToken and burnNativeToken act on the caller's own balance and require membership of the native token owner set. On all three chains getNativeTokenManagementFrom() is 0 and the owner list is empty. Enabling it needs the chain owner and a 7 day delay. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/precompiles/ArbNativeTokenManager.go
- Robinhood Chain, cycle 1. A2: whether Robinhood Stock Token splits and dividends change balanceOf(PoolManager) between or across transactions. Result: Corporate actions change uiMultiplier and leave balanceOf and totalSupply fixed. The token read on chain reports uiMultiplier 1e18 with no pending change. The value per token stays continuous through a split because the multiplier and the share price move in opposite directions, so pools see no jump. Issuer burn and block powers are reported separately as a finding. Evidence: https://docs.robinhood.com/chain/building-with-stock-tokens/
- Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 1. A7 and A4: Stylus programs as hooks or tokens on Robinhood Chain and Elysium. Result: ArbWasm.activationGas() is 2^64-1 on both chains, so no unprivileged caller can activate a Stylus program and a contract with Stylus code that was never activated fails every call. I did not check whether any program was activated before the value was set. If one exists, the Arbitrum One finding applies to it. Evidence: eth_call ArbWasm.activationGas() on https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com and https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz, queried 2026-11-22
- Robinhood Chain, cycle 1. A7 and A10: the 96 KB contract size limit stated in the Robinhood Chain documentation. Result: The PoolManager never reads code size or code of other contracts. Hook permissions come from the address bits (Hooks.sol:337-339) and hook results are checked by length and selector (Hooks.sol:152-166). A larger hook or token contract changes nothing in these paths. Evidence: https://docs.robinhood.com/chain/differences-from-ethereum/
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 1. A10: support and semantics of TSTORE, TLOAD, MCOPY, PUSH0 and SELFBALANCE, and the opcodes whose results differ on Nitro. Result: All three chains are at ArbOS 61. TSTORE, TLOAD and MCOPY arrived with ArbOS 20 and PUSH0 with ArbOS 11. The opcodes that return different values on Nitro are NUMBER, PREVRANDAO, COINBASE and BLOCKHASH, and ASSUMPTIONS.md A10 records that the bytecode uses none of them. I did not disassemble the deployed code myself. Evidence: https://docs.arbitrum.io/run-a-node/arbos-releases/arbos20
- Elysium, cycle 1. A12 on Elysium: the owner path through the Uniswap Wormhole message receiver 0xa9ae0c5eb238a519b7f5af27415eb6dd0744da8d. Result: The receiver accepts messages from 0xf5F4496219F31CDCBa6130B5402873624585615a on Ethereum, whose owner is the Ethereum timelock, verified by a Wormhole core whose guardian set (index 7) is byte-identical to the one on Ethereum. A forged message would need the guardian quorum. The owner can only set the fee controller, so the worst outcome is a protocol fee of 1000 pips per direction and loss of accrued protocol fees. LP principal and claims are out of reach (ProtocolFees.sol:29-57). Evidence: eth_call on https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz and https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com, queried 2026-11-22
- Elysium, cycle 1. A2 and A3 on Elysium: native HYPE and bridged tokens as pool assets. Result: HYPE is the plain native asset with no wrapper or ERC-20 face in the protocol. HyperEVM tokens arrive as standard gateway representations that only the gateway mints and burns, and Elysium-native tokens need no bridge code. The bridges do not support fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens. This rests on the documentation. I did not read the bridge contracts. Evidence: https://elysium.kinetiq.xyz/docs/token-bridging-on-elysium
- Arbitrum One, cycle 1. Transaction filtering and native token management on Arbitrum One. Result: Both features exist in ArbOS 61 and both are off: no filterers, filtering time 0, no native token owners, management time 0. Turning either on needs a chain owner call and a 7 day delay. Evidence: https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc eth_call to ArbOwnerPublic 0x6b, queried 2026-11-22; https://docs.arbitrum.io/run-a-node/arbos-releases/arbos61
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. P1, native take to a special address: does any precompile, predeploy or bridge contract accept value with empty calldata from the PoolManager and return more than the caller is debited. Result: take debits the caller the full amount before the call (PoolManager.sol:294-295, Currency.sol:44-52). Every ArbOS precompile from 0x64 to 0x74, 0xff and 0xa4b05 rejects calldata shorter than 4 bytes, so the take reverts. The Ethereum precompiles 0x02 to 0x08 accept the value and keep it. The wrapped native token mints the same amount to the PoolManager, which is credited to the caller only after a sync of that token and a settle, and the caller still owes the native amount. The WETH and WHYPE gateways accept the value and credit nothing. EntryPoint 0.7 on Robinhood Chain books the value as a deposit of the PoolManager, which a sync and settle can turn into a credit under the EntryPoint address as currency, and that currency can never be taken because the EntryPoint has no transfer function. In each case the caller pays the full value that left. Evidence: eth_call and eth_simulateV1 on https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc, https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com and https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz, queried 2026-11-22; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/precompiles/precompile.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. P2, P3 and P4 with a special address as currency: can transfer succeed while moving something the caller is not debited for, or can balanceOf rise between sync and settle without a payment. Result: No ArbOS precompile has a function with the transfer or balanceOf selector, and all of them revert on both calls. sha256, ripemd and identity return 32 or more bytes for balanceOf, so sync succeeds with a constant and settle pays zero (PoolManager.sol:358-360). Their transfer result is not the value 1, so take reverts (Currency.sol:64-74). ecrecover and P256VERIFY return empty data on the transfer calldata, so take succeeds and moves nothing, the caller is debited, and the debt cannot be repaid because sync reverts on empty return data (Currency.sol:94). The remaining Ethereum precompiles fail on the input. Evidence: eth_call with from set to the PoolManager on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-precompile-interfaces/main/ArbSys.sol and the 17 other interface files
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. P5, a special address as hook: which special addresses pass isValidHookAddress, and what do they return to the IHooks calls. Result: Of the swept addresses only 0x10, 0x64, 0x70, 0x74, 0xc8, 0x100 and 0x800 have a valid flag combination (Hooks.sol:109-127). 0x10 fails with invalid input length on every call shape, 0x64, 0x70 and 0x74 revert on the unknown selector, and 0xc8, 0x100 and 0x800 return empty data or fail, which callHook rejects (Hooks.sol:152-154). A pool with such a hook has the flagged action blocked for good. For 0x100 the flagged action is liquidity removal, which is the case already recorded for hook addresses without code in the accounting unit of cycle 1. The identity precompile echoes the selector but 0x04 has an invalid flag combination (Hooks.sol:112). No special address returns a delta. Evidence: eth_call with from set to the PoolManager on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22; src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-160
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. A10 and the opcode differential: TSTORE and TLOAD with rollback, CALL with value, CALLVALUE, SELFBALANCE, STATICCALL, RETURNDATASIZE, MCOPY, PUSH0, gas forwarding, calls to addresses without code and precompile dispatch. Result: The pinned client implements TSTORE, TLOAD and Call as upstream go-ethereum does, with gas accounting additions only. Eight probes run with eth_call and state overrides returned the same words on Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium and Ethereum, apart from the ArbOS precompile address, which exists only on the three Nitro chains and fails there. For Elysium this covers the RPC node, which runs a locally built binary. The sequencer could not be probed. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/f3a966e/core/vm/eips.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/f3a966e/core/vm/evm.go and eth_call on the three RPC endpoints and https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. A1 at the pinned commit: does any Nitro transaction type run contract code before the transient storage reset, and does a simulated second transaction see the first one's transient storage. Result: StartTxHook runs first and contains no contract call. Transactions that end in the hook run no contract code. For all others StateDB.Prepare replaces the transient map before the call (state_transition.go:636-647 and 737, statedb.go:1599). eth_simulateV1 with a TSTORE in one call and a TLOAD in the next returned zero on all three chains. This confirms the cycle 1 item at the commit the release pins and extends it to Elysium's RPC node. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/f3a966e/core/state_transition.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/arbos/tx_processor.go and eth_simulateV1 on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. A3 faces: every way one balance at the PoolManager can be reached under two currency ids, walked through sync, settle, take, mint and burn in both orders. Result: The only second form of the native asset on each chain is the wrapped token of the Arbitrum token bridge (WETH, WETH, WHYPE). Its balanceOf reads its own storage and its transfer moves no native value, so the two balances are separate. The one cross path the PoolManager can be driven through is a native take to the wrapper, which converts PoolManager native balance into PoolManager wrapped balance one for one. With a prior sync of the wrapper the caller receives a wrapper credit of the amount and owes the same native amount. Without a sync the wrapped tokens become an unaccounted surplus and the caller still owes the native amount. A native settle while the wrapper is synced reverts (PoolManager.sol:356). mint and burn only move claims under the id that was debited or credited. No order yields a credit without an equal payment. Evidence: eth_simulateV1 and eth_call on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22; src/PoolManager.sol:279-364
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. A8 and cross-chain senders: can the PoolManager of the parent chain be driven to send a deposit or a message into the child chain, which would act there under its alias. Result: The parent chain PoolManager can only make calls with empty calldata, transfer, balanceOf, the IHooks selectors and unlockCallback. The Inbox and Bridge of Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain on Ethereum and of Elysium on HyperEVM revert on empty calldata with value and on transfer from the PoolManager address of that chain. They reject plain value, so the path that exists on chains whose deposit contract accepts a bare transfer does not exist here. Evidence: eth_call on https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com and https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm with from set to the PoolManager of that chain, queried 2026-11-22
- Robinhood Chain, cycle 2. Critic lead from cycle 1: what a filter entry identifies, whether entries are added automatically, and whether an ordinary account can make an entry or a rule match another user's PoolManager transaction. Result: An entry is one transaction hash. Entries are added by an automated loop for delayed inbox transactions that touch a restricted address, which is consistent with several thousand entries from one account. A transaction touches an address only as sender, recipient, retryable field, call target, created address, selfdestruct beneficiary, message destination, or as an address in a log topic that a configured event rule names. The restricted list is an off-chain hash list that only the operator's provider changes. In a swap or liquidity change on a pool without attacker-made hook or token, the call targets are the router, Permit2, the PoolManager, the two tokens and the recipient the user named, and the logs come from those contracts with the user, the router and the PoolManager as addresses (PoolManager.sol:145-297). No value in them is chosen by a third party. An attacker who makes the PoolManager call or pay a restricted address through take only gets the attacker's own transaction rejected or hash filtered. The finding therefore stays in the operator class. A pool whose hook or token calls or names a restricted address does block its users, which is the pool-creator class. I did not see the configured event rules or the list itself. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/execution/gethexec/executionengine.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/execution/gethexec/eventfilter/eventfilter.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/f3a966e/arbitrum/filter/filter_report.go and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.11.3/precompiles/ArbFilteredTransactionsManager.go
- Robinhood Chain, cycle 2. A2 on Robinhood Chain: can an ordinary account raise or lower the PoolManager balance of USDG or a stock token without a transfer. Result: mint, burn and adminBurn on the stock token revert for an arbitrary caller with an access control error, and transferFrom needs an allowance that the PoolManager never gives (no approve call exists in src outside the ERC-6909 claims). USDG routes none of 20 reward or claim selectors I tried, and its supply functions sit behind a supply control contract. EIP-3009 transfers need a signature from the holder, which a contract without signature validation cannot give. The USDG facet table could not be listed in full. Evidence: eth_call on https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com, queried 2026-11-22; src/ERC6909.sol:35-56
- Elysium, cycle 2. WHYPE on Elysium: is it a face of HYPE with different units or backing, and can its balance at the PoolManager change without a transfer. Result: The implementation selectors are those of the stock wrapped native token of the Arbitrum token bridge. Total supply equals the native balance of the contract to the wei. bridgeMint and bridgeBurn exist and are tied to the WHYPE gateway reported by l2Gateway(). I did not read verified source, so the gateway restriction rests on the selector set and the documentation. Evidence: eth_call and eth_getBalance on https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz, queried 2026-11-22; https://elysium.kinetiq.xyz/docs/contract-addresses
- Elysium, cycle 2. Elysium mirror bridge: can a bridge wallet or gateway pull tokens out of the PoolManager. Result: The bridge wallet locks a token with transferFrom after the holder approves the wallet. The PoolManager has no function that approves a token spender, so no wallet can pull from it. The bridge factory, bridge wallet gateway, gateway router and ERC-20 gateway revert on every PoolManager call shape. Evidence: https://elysium.kinetiq.xyz/docs/token-bridging-architecture and eth_call on https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. Known weaknesses of the last two years in the Nitro client, ArbOS precompiles and Stylus: can an ordinary account use any of them against funds in the PoolManager. Result: The Security Council report of 2026-10-02 says the known Stylus bugs affect chain liveness and none permits theft, and that they need hand-crafted WASM programs. Activation is closed on all three chains (activationGas is 2^64-1), so no new program can be activated. The one-step proof guard on Arbitrum One delays withdrawals to Ethereum and leaves child chain execution running. The ArbOS 60 double refund in retryable redeems took from the network fee account and never reached a production chain. The Trail of Bits findings for ArbOS 60 and 61 concern consensus determinism and gas pricing. None of these moves a contract's balance or changes call semantics for EVM contracts. A program activated before the pause could still be used for a liveness attack, which I could not rule out. Evidence: https://forum.arbitrum.foundation/t/security-council-emergency-action-2-10-2026/31530, https://docs.arbitrum.io/notices/stylus-activation-pause-notice, https://github.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/pull/4498 and eth_call ArbWasm.activationGas() on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 2. Whether a chain owner switched on native token management, added a transaction filterer or scheduled an ArbOS upgrade since cycle 1. Result: All values are unchanged: no native token owners and management time 0 on all three chains, no filterers on Arbitrum One and Elysium, one filterer on Robinhood Chain, and getScheduledUpgrade() returns zeros everywhere. Evidence: eth_call to ArbOwnerPublic 0x6b on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, cycle 2. Critic lead from cycle 1, second half: does any function an ordinary account can call change balanceOf(PoolManager) on Arbitrum One without a transfer, so that a settle is credited for it. Result: Of 29 token addresses tried, the ones whose balance moves without transfers are four Aave aTokens. Their balance depends on the block timestamp and on the reserve index, and the Aave pool reports that the whole flash loan premium goes to the protocol, so no call inside one transaction raises the index. A sync and a settle in the same transaction therefore see the same balance. The time based growth is recorded as a low finding. The sample is not the full token list of the PoolManager, which I could not obtain. Evidence: eth_call on https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc, queried 2026-11-22; https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-bgd-aave-v3-4/21572
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 3. Critic gap from cycle 2: repeat the special address sweep with a forwarding stub at the PoolManager address, so that each probe is an inner call whose origin is another account, for every target and for the shapes P1, P2, P3, P5 and P7. Result: No target accepts a PoolManager call shape and moves value without an equal debit. Every ArbOS precompile fails on every shape as an inner call too. The only targets whose answer depends on the call depth are 0xc8 and 0xc9, which the node answers itself in a top level RPC call and which are plain addresses on chain (0xc8 holds one byte of code on Arbitrum One), and the CREATE2 deployer, whose balanceOf answer needs a state change and fails under STATICCALL. The targets that accept native value from the PoolManager are addresses without code, the precompiles 0x01 to 0x08 and 0x100, the wrapped native token, the WETH or WHYPE gateway, the three EntryPoints, the PositionManager and the Universal Router. In each case take has already debited the caller the full amount (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295), so the caller is the only party that loses. This is the item recorded as F-048 on other chains. Evidence: https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc, https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com and https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz eth_call with code override at the PoolManager address, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 3. Lead L-203: can a call frame on a Nitro chain carry CALLVALUE that the caller's balance did not pay, through the system caller rule, deposits, retryables or unsigned parent chain messages. Result: No. At the fork commit that Nitro v3.12.4 pins, evm.Call checks the balance and moves the value for every caller, because the system caller branch is disabled on Arbitrum chains until Amsterdam rules (core/vm/evm.go lines 274 to 282 and 322 to 327). On all three live nodes a nested call with 1 ETH from the system address fails when that address holds nothing and moves the balance when it holds 1 ETH. A deposit mints to the sender and moves the value with no call frame (arbos/tx_processor.go lines 237 to 268). A retryable mints the deposit, moves the call value into an escrow account at submission and back to the sender at redeem before an ordinary call (lines 322, 383 to 384 and 554 to 557). Unsigned messages spend the child chain balance of the aliased sender. Native credit in the PoolManager is msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354), so it is always matched by a balance that moved. The live build v3.13.0-rc.9 is not public. The probe covers its behaviour for the system address, and the consensus-v61 module root covers the rest. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/evm.go and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/arbos/tx_processor.go; eth_call probes on the three RPC endpoints, queried 2026-11-22
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 3. Leads L-153 and L-202: does a Stylus host call or a retryable redeem run caller-chosen code inside a running call with a transient storage map other than the caller's, with storage and balance writes kept. Result: No. A Stylus program reads and writes transient storage through the same StateDB map as EVM code, under the address of the acting contract, and its calls go through evm.Call on the same journal (arbos/programs/api.go lines 119 to 128 and 186 to 190). The PoolManager never delegates to other code, so no Stylus program can act under its address. ArbRetryableTx.redeem can be called from inside any call, and it only emits an event. The retry runs after the outer transaction as a transaction of its own, and StateDB.Prepare gives it an empty transient map (arbos/tx_processor.go lines 924 to 956, arbos/block_processor.go lines 426 to 436 and 680 to 719, core/state_transition.go line 950, core/state/statedb.go line 1650). An unlock is one call frame (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), so a redeem can neither run inside it nor see its deltas. The node interface contracts that run nested simulations exist only in RPC calls. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/arbos/programs/api.go, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/arbos/tx_processor.go and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/state_transition.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 3. Lead L-166: is there an address that answers balanceOf(PoolManager) from a ledger which a plain value transfer or a zero amount call from the PoolManager raises, and that answers transfer(address,uint256) by releasing value at a rate other than one for one. Result: None found among the swept targets. The wrapped native token of each chain has both halves and exchanges one for one, with both legs booked (cycle 2). EntryPoint 0.6, 0.7 and 0.8 credit a deposit ledger on plain value and answer balanceOf from it, and they have no transfer function. The PositionManager answers balanceOf with a count of position tokens and has no transfer(address,uint256). No precompile or system address answers either call. The sweep covers system addresses, the token bridge contracts and the standard deployments listed in the profiles. It does not cover every application contract on the chains. Evidence: https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc, https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com and https://rpc.elysium.kinetiq.xyz eth_call with code override at the PoolManager address, queried 2026-11-22
- Elysium, cycle 3. Lead L-135: does the state of Elysium follow the Nitro state transition code although the documentation names a separate sequencer stack and the RPC node is a local build. Result: Yes for the state that the rollup contract accepts. The Elysium rollup on HyperEVM pins wasmModuleRoot 0xc10cd7ec6acaf1c441a3f6bd0900ad20f15855ba775a96f1939118cbc629dc97, the root of the official consensus-v61 replay binary, which the rollups of Arbitrum One and Robinhood Chain pin as well. A sequencer only orders transactions, and each node derives state by executing them. A block that departs from ArbOS 61 semantics would fail validation against that root. The commit of the RPC binary remains unknown, and validation is limited to listed validators, which is an operator matter. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call wasmModuleRoot() on 0x508C173dFe5F737B3493195Bf785d71fA76fD217, queried 2026-11-22; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/Dockerfile line 206
- Elysium, cycle 3. Lead L-136: the Elysium Bridge on HyperEVM executes calls chosen by child chain accounts. Can a call to a HyperCore system address or to CoreWriter take HYPE that backs balances on Elysium, including the HYPE in the PoolManager. Result: No path found. The Bridge sends native value only as part of an outbox call, and the value of that call equals what the sender burned on Elysium. A withdrawal addressed to 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 would credit the HyperCore account of the Bridge, and any Elysium account could later move that HyperCore balance by a message that makes the Bridge call CoreWriter, since CoreWriter accepts actions from the Bridge address. Only the sender of the misdirected withdrawal loses. No CoreWriter action moves the native balance that an address holds on HyperEVM, and the Bridge has no HyperCore account, no HYPE spot balance and no wrapped HYPE today. I did not read the HyperEVM node source, and I did not test the finalize EVM contract action. A link of a HyperCore token to the Bridge would need the Bridge to answer transfer and to emit Transfer events, which the stock Nitro Bridge does not do. Evidence: https://rpc.hyperliquid.xyz/evm eth_call with from set to 0x503D572157113fAaaD4DbeD2647Bb10b949216B6 and reads of 0x0801 and 0x0810, queried 2026-11-22; https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/for-developers/hyperevm/interacting-with-hypercore
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 3. Exits, gas: can an ordinary account make a liquidity removal or a swap of another user exceed the transaction gas limit. Result: Removal cannot be made to exceed it. Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop (src/libraries/Pool.sol:146-238) and all three chains allow 32,000,000 gas per transaction, read from ArbGasInfo. A swap pays for each bitmap word and each initialized tick on its way (src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-430). Measured on Arbitrum One, a sweep from tick -201,872 to the lower bound in a spacing 1 pool, 2,677 bitmap words, costs 6.84M gas, which gives roughly 18M for the whole tick range and stays below the limit. An attacker can add dust positions on many ticks at about 100,000 gas each, which costs about 0.000002 ETH per tick at 0.02 gwei, and can so push a swap that crosses more than roughly 1,200 of them past the limit. The swapper can split the swap, because a swap stops at the price limit the caller passes (src/libraries/Pool.sol:322-338 and 344). Liquidity providers are not blocked. The per tick figures are estimates from the measured totals and were not measured tick by tick. Evidence: https://arb1.arbitrum.io/rpc eth_call to the Quoter 0x8928074CA1b241D8Ec02815881c1Af11E8bC5219 and to ArbGasInfo 0x6c on all three endpoints, queried 2026-11-22

Exits, storage pricing: does ArbOS 61 price storage growth apart from computation, so that one account can raise the price of liquidity operations for others. Result: Not today. getMultiGasPricingConstraints() returns an empty array on all three chains and getMultiGasBaseFee() returns the same fee in every dimension. Only the single gas constraints apply, and raising the base fee through them means paying for the gas that fills the target, as on Ethereum. The Trail of Bits finding about map iteration order in getMultiGasPricingConstraints has nothing to iterate over while the list is empty, and it concerns consensus and not balances. - Robinhood Chain, cycle 3. Exits on Robinhood Chain: can an ordinary account, including one on the restricted list, make the transaction filter reject or fail a transaction of another user on a pool without attacker-made hook or token. Result: No path found. A transaction is filtered for the addresses it touches itself, and cycle 2 showed that a swap or removal on such a pool calls only the PoolManager, the router, the tokens and the recipient the user chose. Two neighbour effects exist in the client and neither reaches other users today. Before v3.11.0 a filtered transaction caused the sequencer to reject clean transactions behind it in the same block, and the changelog records the fix. A user transaction is rolled back together with the redeems it scheduled when one of them touches a filtered address, and the group never includes another user's transaction. The on-chain list holds transaction hashes that only the filterer account can add. The live build v3.13.0-rc.9 is not public, so I could not confirm that the v3.11.0 fix is unchanged in it. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/CHANGELOG.md lines 356 and 527 and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/arbos/block_processor.go
- Robinhood Chain, cycle 3. A2 and A5 for USDG on Robinhood Chain, which pays claimable rewards: can an ordinary account raise balanceOf(PoolManager) without a transfer, enrol the PoolManager, or earn rewards with USDG borrowed from the PoolManager inside one transaction. The PoolManager holds 16.83M USDG. Result: No. balanceOf returns the stored balance and rewards are paid only by a claim, which is a transfer from the claim source to a destination named by the claimer or manager of a payout group. The PoolManager is in no payout group and has no pending proposal. Enrolment needs the registrar role, or a proposal by a group's claimer that the account itself accepts by calling acceptRegisterRewardAddress, or a signature of the account that a claimer presents while partner signed registration is switched on. The PoolManager cannot make that call and cannot sign, and partner signed registration is switched off. The multiplier changes only when a daily period boundary passes, and block.timestamp is constant inside a transaction, so shares bought and sold in one transaction earn nothing. A take and return of USDG inside one unlock therefore yields no reward to the borrower. The registrar could enrol the PoolManager. Rewards on its balance would then go to that group's destination and its balance would stay unchanged. That is an issuer action and falls under F-002. I matched the deployed contract to the repository by selectors and views and did not compare bytecode. Evidence: https://rpc.mainnet.chain.robinhood.com eth_call payoutGroupIdOf, getPendingRegistration, isPartnerSignedRegistrationsEnabled, getFacet, queried 2026-11-22; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paxosglobal/paxos-token-contracts/master/contracts/facets/PayoutGroupFacet.sol, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paxosglobal/paxos-token-contracts/master/contracts/ClaimableRewardsBase.sol and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paxosglobal/paxos-token-contracts/master/contracts/lib/MultiplierGrowthLib.sol
- Robinhood Chain, cycle 3. Exits, token limits: does globalTransferSettings() on USDG set a transfer volume or rate limit that an attacker could use up with USDG borrowed from the PoolManager, which would make later payouts from the PoolManager revert. Result: No. The five fields are the reference time and period of the reward multiplier, the switch for partner signed registration, a reserved gap and the pause flag. _transfer reverts only for a zero recipient, a frozen party, an insufficient balance, a pause or an overflow of the packed 64 bit fields, and 64 bits hold 18 trillion USDG. The pause and freeze switches belong to the issuer (F-002). Known weaknesses of the last two years in Nitro, ArbOS and the two newer chains, beyond the items cycle 2 cleared: can an ordinary account use any of them against funds in the PoolManager. Result: None applies. The Trail of Bits review of ArbOS 60 and 61 has one high finding, a map iteration order that can split consensus, and eight informational ones about gas pricing constraints and an error path of the filter. None moves balances. The retryable ordering hazard that Trail of Bits described in 2024 concerns contracts that send several dependent retryables, and the only parent chain messages the PoolManager depends on are single owner calls. The two incidents reported on Robinhood Chain were an accounting bug inside an exchange and trading ahead of a bridge solver, both outside the PoolManager. Timestamps that repeat across blocks, which that commentary notes, do not matter to code that reads no block field. Leads L-117, L-315 and L-400, answered from the filter precompile, its logs and the client source: what an entry identifies, who adds entries and how soon, whether listed transactions share an address, and whether an ordinary account can make a transaction of another user that calls the PoolManager match the filter through a native take of zero or 1 wei to a listed address, a payment of a listed token, or a pool whose hook or currency is a listed contract. Result: An entry is the hash of one transaction that arrived through the delayed inbox. The only filterer, 0xebdc18a1f5c42fc25552ea233facf4054df224b7, adds it a median of 10 blocks before the transaction executes, and the transaction then fails with all gas consumed and no contract code run. 1,389 of 1,491 executed entries name the wallet 0x42607b2e4fde22e83822d4a86ddac58d847dc289 as sender, recipient or calldata argument, and none names the PoolManager or its periphery. A transaction is judged by the addresses it touches itself while it runs. The three levers leave nothing behind that a later transaction of someone else would touch. A take writes a transient delta and makes one call or one transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, src/types/Currency.sol:44-80), so a take to a listed address makes the attacker's own transaction touch that address and stores no address in the PoolManager. A payment of a listed token and a pool with a listed hook or currency involve the listed contract only in transactions that use that token or that pool, and the PoolKey names both (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). A swap or a liquidity change on another pool calls the PoolManager, its two currencies, its hook if any, the caller and the recipient the caller named. The on-chain list holds hashes that only the filterer can add. F-001 stays in the operator class. The public RPC node does not apply the filter to simulated calls, so I could not run the levers against the sequencer's filter, and the restricted list and the event rules are files I cannot read. Can an ordinary account use that to keep other users from withdrawing from the PoolManager. Result: No. The halt stops the reading of delayed inbox messages and nothing else. On 2026-07-15 one retryable submission held the delayed message count at 35,950 for 4,758 seconds while the sequencer produced 47,314 blocks, so transactions sent to the sequencer, which include every take, burn and liquidity removal, went through. Today a filtered message costs its sender a parent chain transaction and delays the messages behind it by the time the filterer needs, a median of 10 blocks. A user who depends on a forced transaction because the sequencer refuses service is in the operator case of F-001. The live build v3.13.0-rc.9 is not public, so the fixes were read at v3.12.4. - Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 6. Transaction types, walked for msg.sender, msg.value and transient storage in unlock, sync, settle and take at Nitro v3.12.4 and fork commit 0e44603: legacy, access list, dynamic fee and set code transactions, blob transactions, deposits (0x64), unsigned (0x65) and contract (0x66) transactions, retries (0x68), retryable submissions (0x69), internal transactions (0x6a), transactions on the on-chain filter list, and the message kinds batch, heartbeat, nonmutating call and compressed transaction. Result: Blob transactions, nonmutating calls, compressed transactions and heartbeats are rejected by the parser. Deposits, retryable submissions and internal transactions end in the start hook: a deposit credits a balance with no call, a submission creates a ticket, and the start block transaction calls only the EIP-2935 history contract after a transient reset. A filtered transaction runs no contract code. Types 0, 1, 2 and 4 and the types 0x65, 0x66 and 0x68 reach StateDB.Prepare, which replaces the transient map, and then one top call whose value the sender's balance pays (a retry is funded from the ticket escrow first). In each of them the PoolManager sees one transaction: Lock, the deltas and the synced currency start at zero (src/libraries/Lock.sol:10-27, src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:15-38), unlock calls back the direct caller (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), settle credits msg.value or the balance change since sync (src/PoolManager.sol:349-365) and take debits before it pays (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). For types 0x65, 0x66 and 0x68 the caller is the aliased parent chain sender. That address holds code on the child chain only if a contract happens to sit at exactly that address, so in practice the callback returns nothing and unlock reverts when the result is decoded, while sync, which needs no unlock, succeeds and its transient values end with the transaction. A set code transaction lets an account with a delegation be the caller and receive the callback, as on Ethereum. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/arbos/parse_l2.go lines 25 to 190, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/v3.12.4/arbos/tx_processor.go lines 197 to 600 and 1066 to 1105, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/state_transition.go lines 837, 950 and 964, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/state_processor.go line 358

Result: codeBitmap marks the data bytes of PUSH1 to PUSH32 with the 8 and 16 byte helpers, which overwrite only bytes for positions not yet visited, and keeps 4 spare bytes for a trailing PUSH32 (core/vm/analysis_legacy.go lines 33 to 118). validJumpdest rejects targets at or past the code end and targets above 2^64, requires a JUMPDEST byte and a code segment (core/vm/contract.go lines 77 to 123). JUMPI tests the whole 256 bit word with IsZero (instructions.go lines 540 to 552). The cache is keyed by the code hash that resolveCodeHash returns, which for a delegated account is the hash of the code that resolveCode runs; the one mismatch, a delegation to a precompile under ArbOS 50 or later, runs no code (evm.go lines 791 to 821). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/analysis_legacy.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/contract.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/evm.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 9. Lead L-577, CALL success flag, RETURNDATACOPY bounds and return data handling at fork commit 0e44603, against src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 and src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134-148. Result: opCall pushes 1 or 0 after the child returns, then copies at most retSize bytes of the child output into memory only on success or revert, and sets the return data buffer to the full output (instructions.go lines 730 to 774). RETURNDATACOPY fails when offset plus length overflows or passes the buffer end (lines 312 to 328). Memory.Set copies the shorter of the two lengths (memory.go lines 52 to 64). The success test of Currency.transfer, which reads the word at 0 only when the return data is 32 bytes or more, and the return data copy of Hooks.callHook therefore see what they see on Ethereum. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/instructions.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/memory.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 9. Stack arena and pooled memory introduced in the fork interpreter: can a nested call, a Stylus program calling back into the EVM, or a pooled buffer change a value the PoolManager computed or the return data it reads. Result: The arena guarantees 1,024 free slots at the start of each frame and grows by reallocation (stack.go lines 55 to 70). Every opcode that runs a child frame pops its arguments by value before the call and pushes through the arena after it, so no pointer into the old backing array is written after a growth. Memory taken from the pool is zeroed up to its length on return and is never shrunk while in use, so a reused buffer exposes only zeros; buffers above 16 KiB are dropped (memory.go lines 25 to 49). Data handed to a child, to a LOG or returned by RETURN and REVERT is a copy or the caller memory that stays unchanged during the child. Stylus programs run through ExecuteWASM with the same arena (interpreter.go lines 168 to 172). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/stack.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/memory.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/interpreter.go

- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 18. Jump destination analysis. codeBitmapInternal in core/vm/analysis_legacy.go:79 of fork 0e44603 decides whether a byte starts push data with the signed comparison int8(op) < int8(PUSH1), so opcodes 0x80 to 0xff are negative and skipped. 605 programs per chain put each of the 256 opcode bytes before a JUMPDEST at distances 0, 1, n-1, n and n+1 for PUSHn and jump to it. Result: All 605 programs give the specified outcome on each chain: the jump succeeds unless the JUMPDEST sits inside PUSHn data, and fails there. The analysis file is byte-identical in 0e44603 and on the fork's master. In the PoolManager bytecode 29 bytes of value 0x5b lie inside push data and no push constant names one as a target, so even a wrong bitmap could not redirect a jump in core. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/018/arbitrum-family.work/raw/jumpdest.json; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/analysis_legacy.go
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 18. Go issue 82839 (open; go1.26.6 to go1.26.10, go1.27.3 and master, a variant from go1.24.13): prove carries a fact through a sign extension of a narrow integer compared with a constant that does not fit the narrow type. Searched holiman/uint256 v1.3.2 (uint256.go, mod.go, div.go, conversion.go, decimal.go) and the fork's core/vm (memory.go, stack.go, instructions.go, interpreter.go, analysis_legacy.go, common.go) and core/state/transient_storage.go for conversions to int8, int16, int32, uint8, uint16 and uint32. Result: Four sites exist and none has the shape. analysis_legacy.go:79 compares two int8 values with the constant 96, which fits int8, and nothing is extended. uint256 ExtendSign (uint256.go:1275) computes uint64(int64(int8(signByte))) with no comparison or branch on the result. mod.go:53 compares a uint32 with 0x80000000, which fits uint32 and is zero-extended. The other uses are byte encodings in uint256.go:118 and 173. SIGNEXTEND, which TickMath and the int24 and int128 casts of the PoolManager depend on, passes 7,921 battery and 2,454 chained vectors on all three chains. Evidence: https://github.com/golang/go/issues/82839; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/holiman/uint256/v1.3.2/uint256.go; research/network-risk/cycles/018/arbitrum-family.work/dl/
- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 18. Shared stack arena of fork 0e44603 (core/vm/stack.go): one arena per EVM, each call frame starts at its parent's top, and stack() grows the slice with slices.Grow when fewer than 1,024 slots remain, while pop1Peek1 and pop2Peek1 hand out pointers into the slice. A parent that kept a pointer across a child call that grew the arena would read stale memory. Programs that push 2, 501 or 1,001 values, recurse to depth 0 to 8 so that every child forces a growth, and sum their own stack after the call. Result: 18 of 18 programs return (d+1)K(K+1)/2 on each chain and on Ethereum. opCall pops its operands by value and pushes its result through the arena pointer after the call (instructions.go:730-774), so no pointer survives a child frame. A PoolManager frame holds at most 49 items while it calls a hook or token, so the parent's values survive a hook or token that fills its own stack. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/018/arbitrum-family.work/raw/arena.json; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/go-ethereum/0e44603/core/vm/stack.go

- Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 18. Can an ordinary account get a parent chain message executed with the PoolManager as sender?. Result: No. The stock Inbox passes every message sender through applyL1ToL2Alias in _deliverToBridge (Inbox.sol:317-324), so a contract or unsigned message with the PoolManager as sender needs a parent chain sender equal to the PoolManager address minus 0x1111000000000000000000000000000000001111, an address nobody holds a key or creation path for. The three ToFork functions undo the alias for an EOA caller, but they revert unless the parent chain id has changed, and the unsigned transaction they produce keeps the EOA check, which the PoolManager's code fails. Deposits credit the native balance without running code and are not a payment in settle, which reads msg.value (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364). Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro-contracts/main/src/bridge/Inbox.sol; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OffchainLabs/nitro/master/arbos/parse_l2.go; src/PoolManager.sol:349-364

Result: getScheduledUpgrade() returns zeros on all three chains (blocks 527,731,261, 123,614,656 and 11,033,107) and arbOSVersion is 116 (ArbOS 61) everywhere. No proposal for a version after 61 was found. Glamsterdam has no mainnet date. If its execution changes reached ArbOS they would not reach pool funds: the deterministic factory predeploy of EIP-7997 at 0x12 is not a valid hook address because its low bits set AFTER_ADD_LIQUIDITY_RETURNS_DELTA without AFTER_ADD_LIQUIDITY (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:113), and as a currency it cannot answer sync because a CREATE inside the staticcall of balanceOf fails; the GAS change of EIP-8037 only touches the forwarded budget at Currency.sol:48 and 73 and Hooks.sol:134; the instructions of EIP-8024 are covered by F-145. The Elysium HyperCore upgrade is still unscheduled and is held by L-770. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/025/arbitrum-family.work/raw/arbos_state.txt; https://ethereum.org/en/roadmap/glamsterdam/; https://elysium.kinetiq.xyz/docs/what-is-elysium
- Arbitrum One, cycle 25. Priority gas auctions on Arbitrum One, which replaced Timeboost: whether ordering by priority fee lets an ordinary account reach other users' funds in the PoolManager. Result: Ordering decides only which transaction runs first. Each unlock runs to completion inside one transaction and reverts as a whole unless every delta is settled (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114), and the mempool stays private, so an account can pay to run before or after a visible transaction from the feed but cannot see pending ones or insert work inside another account's unlock. What a later swap loses to an earlier one is bounded by the price limit and the router's minimum amount, as on Ethereum. Evidence: https://docs.arbitrum.io/how-arbitrum-works/timeboost
- Robinhood Chain, cycle 26. Lead L-1109: does Nitro rc.9 b72783f give the specified word on the targeted set, the battery and script set 1 when the answer comes from the linux-amd64 backend of Robinhood Chain, which had no targeted or pmdiff run. Result: Robinhood Chain's endpoint routes every request, and every element of a batch, to an amd64 or an arm64 backend on its own (three-element web3_clientVersion batches came back mixed, raw/clientversion.txt), so a bracket cannot pin one eth_call. Each batch was therefore sent several times, each send bracketed. targeted.py: 143 batches of 600 vectors sent 8 times each (1,144 eth_calls), 0 mismatches; every batch had at least two sends with an amd64 bracket and 127 had a send with amd64 on both sides. battery.py: 167 batches sent 6 times (1,002 eth_calls), 0 mismatches, 167 of 167 with an amd64 bracket. pmdiff.py with this checkout's build (code sha256 equal to cycle 25's a7aaa3ba): 250 scripts sent 8 times (2,000 eth_calls), every answer identical to the cycle 25 Ethereum reference hash, 226 scripts with an amd64-amd64 bracketed send. The brackets read amd64 4,155 times and arm64 4,135 times, so with independent routing near one half the chance that a given targeted batch never reached amd64 in 8 sends is 1/256 and for a pmdiff script in 8 sends 1/256. No arithmetic, jump, memory or PoolManager result differs between the two architectures, so the lines of FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, TickMath and BitMath that these vectors and scripts drive compute the same on both. - Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, cycle 32. What the PoolManager's take and sync shapes do against the P256VERIFY precompile at 0x100, ArbSys (0x64) and ArbRetryableTx (0x6e), called from the PoolManager address by eth_call. Result: 0x100 returns success with empty data for both transfer(address,uint256) and balanceOf(address); 0x64 and 0x6e revert with empty data for both. For a currency of 0x100, take passes the success check of src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 because return data is empty, but no value leaves the PoolManager and the caller is debited the full amount in that currency (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). sync reverts because the high-level balanceOf call in Currency.sol:94 cannot decode empty return data, so no credit can be created in that currency by settle (PoolManager.sol:349-365). Ethereum has the same precompile at the same address since Osaka, so this is no difference from Ethereum. A pool naming such a currency is in the class of an attacker-chosen token and holds no value of other users. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/032/arbitrum-family.work/raw/special_calls.txt

## Reading of the source (accounting)

- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Whether the four fixed transient slots match their stated derivations and whether a per account delta slot can collide with them. Result: I computed keccak256 of 'ReservesOf', 'Currency', 'NonzeroDeltaCount' and 'Unlocked' minus one with a keccak implementation written for this review. All four equal the constants in the source. Delta slots are keccak256 of the 64 byte pair (target, currency), and getDelta and applyDelta pass the arguments to _computeSlot in the same order, so a collision with a fixed slot or between two pairs needs a hash collision. Evidence: src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:10-13; src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:8-10; src/libraries/Lock.sol:7-8; src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Sign and direction of every delta, which account is credited or debited, and whether unlock can return with an open delta. Result: take and mint debit msg.sender (PoolManager.sol:294, 326). settle credits the named recipient with msg.value or with the checked balance increase since sync (349-364). burn credits msg.sender and burns from an account that _burnFrom checks for operator status or allowance (332-336, ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). clear removes only an exact positive delta (310-319). donate debits the donor (268-270, Pool.sol:471). Swap and liquidity deltas go to msg.sender after the hook share is split off (181-183, 224-226). _accountDelta adds with checked int256 arithmetic and moves the nonzero counter only on a transition to or from zero (368-378, CurrencyDelta.sol:37). unlock reverts unless the counter is zero and then clears the flag (112-113). I found no path that creates a positive delta without a payment, a burned claim or a matching pool obligation. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 291-378; src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:28-41; src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Access control on every external function of the PoolManager, and what the owner and the fee controller can reach. Result: unlock, initialize, sync and the ERC-6909 token functions are open by design. modifyLiquidity, swap, donate, take, settle, settleFor, clear, mint and burn require the unlocked flag. updateDynamicLPFee requires msg.sender to be the pool's hook and a dynamic fee pool. setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees require msg.sender to be protocolFeeController. setProtocolFeeController uses onlyOwner from solmate Owned. The controller can set a fee of at most 1000 pips per direction and can withdraw at most protocolFeesAccrued, with a checked subtraction. src has no upgrade, pause or general withdrawal function. lib/solmate is an empty directory in this checkout, so I could not read Owned.sol; a fetch of the pinned file was refused by this session's permission system. As a substitute I ran read only calls on all 21 deployed PoolManagers: storage slot 0 equals the owner and slot 2 equals the fee controller recorded in networks.json, setProtocolFeeController and transferOwnership from a random address revert with an Error(string), and collectProtocolFees from a random address reverts with InvalidCaller (0x48f5c3ed). That shows the deployed contracts gate these functions. It does not show which Owned.sol the CTF build will compile against. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:96-99, 339-346; src/ProtocolFees.sol:29-57; src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8-32; rpc: eth_call and extsload reads against the PoolManager address on each of the 21 rpc URLs in research/network-risk/state/networks.json, run 2026-11-22
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Whether sync, which runs while the manager is locked and whose result survives after unlock returns, lets one party collect a credit for tokens another party paid, under the rule that transient storage is cleared at the end of each transaction. Result: After unlock returns, the lock flag is false and every delta is zero. The synced currency and reserves are the only transient values that can remain. A credit from settle is the balance increase since the most recent sync of that currency (PoolManager.sol:358-360), sync overwrites both slots (286) and an ERC-20 settle resets the currency (361). A payer that syncs immediately before its transfer and settles immediately after leaves no window for another party. A stale sync by an earlier party can only make a later native settle with value revert (356) or make the later party's own sync replace it. The balance can also not fall between sync and settle through fee collection of that ERC-20 (ProtocolFees.sol:49-52), and a take in between makes settle revert on the checked subtraction (360). This holds only while transient storage is cleared between transactions (EIP-1153). If a network kept transient storage across transactions, a party could sync a token, wait, and later settle the whole net inflow since that sync; see the lead on this. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364; src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32; https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1153
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Whether calling collectProtocolFees while the manager is unlocked, at a moment chosen by an unprivileged party through a permissionless fee controller, can move funds to that party or strand another party's payment. This answers the leads raised by the ethereum-reference, established-l1, arbitrum-family and high-throughput units. Result: My reading agrees with theirs. The function lowers protocolFeesAccrued and the balance by the same amount and sends the tokens to the recipient the controller names. It changes no delta. Collection of an ERC-20 that is currently synced reverts in both lock states, so the settle that follows a sync cannot be shortened. Native settlement uses msg.value and no balance reading. On a network where an ERC-20 mirrors the native balance, collecting native fees while that ERC-20 is synced is not blocked by the check at ProtocolFees.sol:49, and it would lower the next settle of that ERC-20 by the collected amount. The party that pays for that is whoever settles next after its own sync, and a payer who syncs, transfers and settles without an external call in between cannot be interleaved. I found no gain for the caller. Evidence: src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57; src/PoolManager.sol:349-364
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Code level check of a native asset that also has an ERC-20 face whose balanceOf mirrors the native balance: can one deposit be credited twice, once as address(0) and once as the ERC-20. Result: A native credit needs the synced currency to be address(0) and uses msg.value (PoolManager.sol:353-354). An ERC-20 credit needs that ERC-20 to be synced and rejects any msg.value (356). The two conditions exclude each other inside one settle call. The PoolManager has no receive or fallback function, so settle and settleFor are the only calls that can carry value. I walked the orders sync, take, transfer and settle across both faces: each unit that enters is credited once in one currency id and each unit that leaves is debited once. test/Sync.t.sol:255-275 expects the same revert. Whether a network has such a token, and what else can move its balance, is for the network units. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 349-364; test/Sync.t.sol:255-275
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. A currency address with no code (A4): can take or mint create value from it. Result: take on a codeless currency returns success and moves nothing (Currency.sol:64-74), and it debits the caller. A credit needs settle, and settle needs sync, which calls balanceOf through a high level call. Solidity skips the extcodesize check there only because it decodes the return data, and decoding empty return data reverts. So no positive delta and no ERC-6909 claim can be created for a codeless currency, and a pool on it can hold no liquidity. If code is removed from a token after deposits, takes report success while delivering nothing; that case depends on the network and is covered under A7. Evidence: src/types/Currency.sol:40-96; src/PoolManager.sol:279-288; https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.26/control-structures.html
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Order of state updates around external calls: native and ERC-20 payouts, hook calls, the unlock callback and fee collection. Result: take records the debit before the transfer (PoolManager.sol:294-295). collectProtocolFees lowers the accrued amount before the transfer (ProtocolFees.sol:55-56). Pool state is read after the before hooks return (PoolManager.sol:156-159, 202-206, 266-268) and is fully written before the after hooks run. A hook or payee that re-enters meets consistent state and only adds deltas of its own, which it must settle. The ERC-20 transfer assembly evaluates the call before it reads returndatasize, as its comment says, because Yul evaluates arguments right to left. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:145-297; src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56; src/types/Currency.sol:64-74; https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.26/yul.html
- all 21 networks, cycle 1. Hook return deltas: can a hook move value out of a pool it is not attached to, or change the pool's own obligations. Result: In every hook path the caller's delta is the pool delta minus the hook delta and the hook is credited the hook delta (Hooks.sol:230, 242, 305-313; PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226), so the two always sum to what the pool computed. The beforeSwap specified delta changes the amount sent to the pool and is rejected if it flips exact input to exact output or back (Hooks.sol:273-279). Return deltas are read only when the matching flag bit is set, and those bits are rejected at initialize unless the action bit is set too (Hooks.sol:109-120). The fee override is used only for dynamic fee pools and is validated against 1,000,000 (Hooks.sol:263, Pool.sol:303-305). Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:109-127, 209-315; src/PoolManager.sol:177-227

Second independent line by line read of the 18 files of this unit: sign and direction of every delta, rounding direction of every math step, comparison operators, bounds on ticks, prices, fees and liquidity, unchecked blocks, casts and assembly. Result: I found no line in these files that lets a caller take funds or block a withdrawal for a token whose supply in base units is below 2^127. Amounts owed by a caller round up and amounts paid to a caller round down in SqrtPriceMath.getAmount0Delta and getAmount1Delta (signed versions at lines 261-288), in SwapMath.computeSwapStep (input with roundUp true at lines 66-68 and 100-102, output with roundUp false at lines 84-90) and in Position.update (floor at lines 93-96). Pool.swap debits the specified side and credits the calculated side with the signs the PoolManager expects (Pool.sol:371-382, 451-462), crosses a tick with the fee growth of the input currency taken from the running value (416-420) and negates liquidityNet only when moving left (424). updateTick and getFeeGrowthInside use the same convention for growth below a tick (535, 498-509). Whether the int128 casts on liquidity amounts and fees can stop a withdrawal for an ordinary token, and whether the fee cast revert reported by the accounting unit can be reached without paying 2^127 base units. Result: A removal whose amount in one currency is 2^127 or more reverts in toInt128 at Pool.sol:212-234. The amount scales with liquidityDelta, so the owner can remove the position in smaller parts. In the 28,000 fuzz sequences three final removals reverted for this reason (seeds 12742, 13908 and 111494, all at extreme prices), each succeeded after the liquidity delta was halved once, and every position was fully withdrawn. If principal plus fees overflows in the BalanceDelta addition at PoolManager.sol:171, a zero delta call collects the fees first. The remaining case is the fee amount itself at Pool.sol:192. Fee growth inside a range rises only while slot0.tick is inside the range, when the position's liquidity is part of pool liquidity, and each rise is floor(fee * 2^128 / liquidity) (Pool.sol:404-405, 474-477). The amount owed to a position is therefore at most the fees and donations actually paid while it was in range. A donor who also holds a large position in the same range gets back only that position's share, so the donor's net cost equals what the other positions are owed. Borrowing through take does not help, because the borrowed amount has to be repaid in the same unlock. The solvency check of the fuzz covers the same statement. The fee cast revert therefore needs 2^127 base units of one currency given up by payers, which is possible only for a token whose supply in base units exceeds 2^127 or whose balanceOf is under the attacker's control. A9, gas caps against the loops in the pool math: can a block or transaction gas cap stop liquidity providers from withdrawing, on HyperEVM with 3,000,000 gas blocks in particular. Result: Pool.modifyLiquidity has no loop. It updates two ticks, at most two bitmap words, one position and the pool liquidity (Pool.sol:159-236). The repository's own gas snapshots, which I did not re-measure, record 130,613 gas for a removal with an empty hook, 161,276 for a simple add and 292,593 for a new salted position, all through test routers. These are far below the smallest cap in networks.json. On HyperEVM, 80 of the 81 blocks from 51,944,427 to 51,944,507 had a gas limit of 3,000,000 and one had 30,000,000, which agrees with the dual block documentation. The only loop is in Pool.swap (Pool.sol:344-437). It advances one bitmap word per step when no tick is initialized, and a pool with tick spacing 1 has 6,932 words across the whole tick range. The snapshots give about 2,250 gas for the bitmap lookup and 900 to 1,600 gas for computeSwapStep per step, and I did not measure getSqrtPriceAtTick or loop overhead, so a full traversal is in the tens of millions of gas. That exceeds a HyperEVM small block and probably the 16,777,216 gas transaction cap of EIP-7825 where that cap is active. I did not confirm on which of the 21 networks EIP-7825 is active. The loop ends when the price reaches the caller's limit (Pool.sol:344), so a long move can be split over several transactions, and no withdrawal depends on a swap. A gas cap can make large single transaction swaps fail. It cannot freeze liquidity through the code in these files.
