## Reading of the source (flow-swap)

- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Line by line trace of a swap in a pool without a hook, from PoolManager.swap to the last delta written, for exact input and exact output in both directions. Result: swap rejects a zero amount and an uninitialized pool before anything else (src/PoolManager.sol:193-196). With hooks equal to address(0) beforeSwap returns the caller's amount unchanged and afterSwap returns a zero hook delta, because no permission bit is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:252-255, 298, 306). Pool.swap treats a negative amount as exact input and a positive amount as exact output at every place that branches on it (src/libraries/Pool.sol:313, 371, 453; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:61). For exact input the remaining amount rises toward zero by amountIn plus fee and the calculated amount grows by amountOut. For exact output the remaining amount falls by amountOut and the calculated amount falls by amountIn plus fee (Pool.sol:371-382). The final delta puts the specified amount in currency1 exactly when zeroForOne differs from exact input (Pool.sol:453-461), so the caller is debited the input currency and credited the output currency in all four cases. Both casts to int128 revert on overflow (Pool.sol:455, 459; src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). The protocol fee is booked to the input currency (PoolManager.sol:216, 238). _accountPoolBalanceDelta writes amount0 to currency0 and amount1 to currency1 for msg.sender (PoolManager.sol:226, 381-384). I found no step where a sign, an operand order or a cast gives the caller more than the pool math computed. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:187-253, 368-384; src/libraries/Pool.sol:279-463; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:51-107
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. beforeSwap: the returned delta, the check that the swap type does not change, and the fee override word, including a hook that returns dirty upper bits. Result: The hook result must be exactly 96 bytes and start with the beforeSwap selector, otherwise the call reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154, 259). The specified delta is read only when the address carries BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG (Hooks.sol:266-270). It is added to the caller's amount with checked arithmetic, and the call reverts when an exact input amount becomes positive or an exact output amount becomes negative (Hooks.sol:273-278). An amount of exactly zero is allowed and makes Pool.swap return a zero delta without touching state (src/libraries/Pool.sol:320). The fee word is read only for a dynamic fee pool (Hooks.sol:263). parseFee assigns a full 32 byte word to a uint24 in assembly (src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:16-21). The value is then used only through isOverride, which ANDs with 0x400000, and removeOverrideFlag, which ANDs with 0xBFFFFF, followed by a comparison with 1,000,000 (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, Pool.sol:303-305). Both masks are 24 bit constants, so upper bits supplied by the hook cannot reach the fee, whatever the compiler does with the assignment. Without the override bit the stored fee is used. A hook can set the fee of its own dynamic fee pool to any value from 0 to 100 percent, which is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and does not reach pools without that hook. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:248-282; src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:9-28; src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78; src/libraries/Pool.sol:300-320
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. afterSwap and the two _accountDelta calls: does the caller delta plus the hook delta always equal the pool delta, and can a cast or a packing step lose a value. Result: afterSwap takes the specified and unspecified parts of the beforeSwap return, adds the afterSwap return to the unspecified part with a checked int128 cast and a checked addition (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:295-303), places the two parts in currency order with the same rule that Pool.swap uses (Hooks.sol:307-309 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:453), and subtracts the hook delta from the swap delta (Hooks.sol:312). The subtraction works on sign extended halves and reverts when a half leaves the int128 range (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46). PoolManager.swap then credits the hook delta to the hook address and the remainder to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:221-226). The pool was run with the adjusted amount, so the two accounts together receive exactly the pool delta and each must reach zero before unlock returns (PoolManager.sol:112). I transcribed these lines and ran 20,000 random combinations of direction, amount and hook delta. Caller plus hook equalled the pool delta in every accepted case, and the accepted and rejected cases matched the conditions written in test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:195-209. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:284-315; src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-71; src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37; src/PoolManager.sol:220-227, 368-384
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Fee split between protocol and liquidity providers in each step, and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share. Result: The swap fee is the LP fee when the protocol fee is zero and protocolFee + lpFee - floor(protocolFee * lpFee / 1e6) otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:307, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). It equals the protocol fee only when the LP fee is zero, because the protocol fee field is 12 bits wide and capped at 1,000. In that case the whole step fee goes to the protocol. Otherwise the protocol receives floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * protocolFee / 1e6) and the rest goes to fee growth (Pool.sol:391-405). In 300,000 random step shapes over the whole price range, with liquidity from 0 to 2^127 and amounts up to 2^255, the protocol share never exceeded the step fee, so the unchecked subtraction at Pool.sol:395 did not wrap. The transcribed swap reproduced the protocol fee totals that test/PoolManager.t.sol:779-818 and test/DynamicFees.t.sol:286-318 expect in 12,000 random cases, including the rounding up when the LP fee is zero. Rounding favours liquidity providers over the protocol and never the swapper. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:283-308, 384-407; src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:17-46; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Rounding of every amount in a swap step, asking who gains if a result is off by one unit. Result: Exact input: the amount after fee is rounded down, the input needed to reach the target is rounded up, the fee on a full step is rounded up, the fee on a partial step is the whole remainder, and the output is rounded down (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:64-86). Exact output: the output to the target is rounded down, the input and the fee are rounded up (SwapMath.sol:88-104). The next price is rounded up when currency0 comes in and down when currency1 comes in, which moves the price less than the exact result for an input and more for an output (src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-120, 146-148, 175-177). Every rounding step is against the swapper. The transcription returned the values asserted in test/libraries/SwapMath.t.sol:69-180 for seven fixed vectors and the Swap event values asserted in test/DynamicFees.t.sol:156-279, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol:94, test/PoolManager.t.sol:501-503 and 608. Evidence: src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:51-107; src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-289; src/libraries/FullMath.sol:14-116; src/libraries/UnsafeMath.sol:12-28
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Tick crossing, the sign of liquidityNet, the tick stored after a step, and the price limit bounds. Result: The loop asks the bitmap for the next tick at or below the current tick when zeroForOne and above it otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:347-348, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:94-119), clamps the result to MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK (Pool.sol:351-356) and uses the nearer of that tick's price and the limit as the target (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:25-36). A crossing happens only when the step ends exactly on the price of an initialized tick. It flips both fee growth outside values with the updated growth of the input currency and applies liquidityNet with its sign reversed for zeroForOne (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). After a zeroForOne step that ends on a tick the stored tick is one below it (Pool.sol:431). I traced the following oneForZero swap, a liquidity add on each side of that tick and a donate from that state. Each of them treats the pool as sitting just below the tick, which agrees with the liquidity value the swap left. A zeroForOne limit must be above MIN_SQRT_PRICE and a oneForZero limit below MAX_SQRT_PRICE (Pool.sol:322-338), so a swap cannot cross MIN_TICK downward or reach the price of MAX_TICK. Addition of liquidityNet reverts above 2^128 - 1 (src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19) and the per tick cap keeps the sum over all ticks below that bound (Pool.sol:165-173, 565-582). The transcription returned the next tick and the initialized flag asserted in 19 fixed cases of test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol:130-293 and met its two fuzz properties in 40,000 random cases. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:322-359, 409-449, 596-612; src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:16-121; src/libraries/TickMath.sol:57-237
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Extremes of tick, price, liquidity, amount and fee, tested as solvency of one pool: can any sequence make a pool pay out more of a currency than it took in. This matters for every pool, because the PoolManager keeps no reserve per pool and a pool that overpays would draw on the balances of the others. Result: I wrote a third transcription of FullMath, UnsafeMath, BitMath, TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, LiquidityMath, TickBitmap, the position update and Pool.initialize, modifyLiquidity, swap and donate from the source text, with 256 bit wrapping where the source is unchecked or assembly. I checked it against the fixed values in the repository tests named in the other items. I then ran 8,000 random sequences of 5 to 40 operations: tick spacings 1, 10, 60, 200, 32767 and random, starting prices over the whole range including MIN_TICK and the ticks next to MAX_TICK, static fees from 0 to 100 percent, a per swap fee override in 40 percent of the swaps, protocol fees from 0 to 1,000 in both directions, liquidity up to 2^126, exact input and exact output amounts up to 2^255 with both the extreme and nearby price limits, and donations up to 2^126. After every operation, and after all positions were removed, the net amount the pool had received in each currency was at least the protocol fee accrued, in all 8,000 runs. 17 runs ended with a position that could not be removed. In each of them the fees paid into the pool in one currency exceeded 2^127 base units, which is the recorded finding F-005 and cannot happen for a token whose supply is below 2^127. Evidence: src/libraries/Pool.sol:94-612; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:20-107; src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-289; src/libraries/TickMath.sol:57-237; src/libraries/Position.sol:76-102
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Zero liquidity in range: a swap step with liquidity 0 moves the price for free. Can that give the swapper tokens or damage positions. Result: With liquidity 0 the input to the target, the output and the fee are all 0, the step reaches its target and no fee growth is added (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:66-74, 84-90; src/libraries/Pool.sol:401). In the transcription a swap of 1e18 exact input through an empty range returned the delta (0, 0) and only moved the price and tick. Positions are not affected, because a later add or removal computes its amounts from the price and tick of that moment with the usual rounding (Pool.sol:206-237) and the solvency runs above include such moves. The free move matters for contracts that read a pool price as an oracle and for the gas cost recorded in the finding of this unit. It does not move funds in core. Evidence: src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105; src/libraries/Pool.sol:344-437
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Swap hook calls to an address that is a precompile, a system contract or an account without code: can the PoolManager be made to accept such a call during a swap. Result: callHook reverts unless the call succeeds and the return data is at least 32 bytes that start with the selector that was sent (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). An address without code returns nothing and fails this test. beforeSwap also needs exactly 96 bytes (Hooks.sol:259) and afterSwap with the return delta flag exactly 64 bytes (Hooks.sol:166). A contract that returns its input unchanged passes the selector test but returns the whole call data, which is longer than 96 bytes for beforeSwap and longer than 64 bytes for afterSwap, so it cannot act as a swap hook that returns deltas. It can only pass as an afterSwap hook without the return delta flag, where the return value is ignored (Hooks.sol:163). A failed hook call reverts the whole swap, so a side effect in the callee does not survive. Such a pool is one that somebody chose to create with that address as hook, and pools without a hook never make these calls. Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-168, 248-315
- Celo, Polygon, Arc, cycle 2. A native asset that also answers as an ERC-20 at some address: can sync, settle and take, in any order, credit one payment twice or credit more than was paid. Exhaustive search over a model of src/PoolManager.sol:279-297 and 349-364. Result: I modelled the PoolManager balance, the synced currency, the synced reserves, the two deltas and the attacker's wallet, with operations sync(0), sync(face), settle with value, settle without value, take in each currency, a transfer through the face and a native transfer that reaches the PoolManager without a call. I searched every sequence of up to 6 operations with amounts 1, 2 and 3. When the face reports the native balance one to one, no sequence left the attacker better off. The guard at PoolManager.sol:356 blocks the only order that would count a value twice. When the face reports floor(native / S) for S above 1, the best sequence gained S - 1 base units per round of sync and settle, and it needs native value to arrive without a call while the face is synced. On Arc the USDC contract at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 returns decimals 6 and its balanceOf for the PoolManager equalled floor(eth_getBalance / 1e12) at blocks 0x1f14a00, 0x1f14a63 and 0x1f14a79, with remainders of 930109466545, 178438878313 and 971982015932 base units. S is therefore 1e12 there and one round can gain less than 0.000001 USDC. I did not test whether native USDC can reach the PoolManager without a call on Arc, and I did not query the one to one property on Celo and Polygon again. For those two I rely on the earlier findings F-023 and F-008. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-364; https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io eth_call decimals() and balanceOf(PoolManager) on 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 and eth_getBalance at blocks 0x1f14a00, 0x1f14a63, 0x1f14a79

## Reading of the source (invariants-bits)

- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Slot0 packing: field offsets, mask widths, sign handling of the tick and the effect of dirty upper bits passed to a setter. Result: The four fields sit at bit offsets 0, 160, 184 and 208 with widths 160, 24, 24 and 24, so they end at bit 232 and do not overlap (src/types/Slot0.sol:33-38). MASK_160_BITS is written with 42 hex digits, two of them leading zeros, and equals 2^160 - 1. Every setter ANDs the new value with its mask before the shift and clears only its own field in the packed word (Slot0.sol:66-93). The tick getter sign extends from 24 bits (Slot0.sol:47-51). I transcribed the eight functions into Python and ran 200,000 random cases in which each setter received a full 256 bit value. Every getter returned the input truncated to the field width, the top 24 bits of the word stayed unchanged, and the order of the setters did not change the result. No caller-supplied value can spill into a neighbouring field. The repository test test/types/Slot0.t.sol:8-35 states the same round trip and the source text satisfies it. Evidence: src/types/Slot0.sol:33-93; test/types/Slot0.t.sol:8-35
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. BalanceDelta and BeforeSwapDelta packing and unpacking, and the arithmetic on packed deltas. Result: toBalanceDelta shifts amount0 left by 128 bits and masks amount1 to 128 bits, so sign extension bits of a negative amount1 cannot reach amount0 (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-18). amount0 is read with sar 128 and amount1 with signextend 15 (BalanceDelta.sol:61-71). add and sub split both operands, add or subtract the halves as 256 bit numbers and pass each half through SafeCast.toInt128, which reverts when the result leaves the int128 range (BalanceDelta.sol:20-46, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). A carry from the low half therefore cannot enter the high half. BeforeSwapDelta uses the same layout with the specified amount in the high half (src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37). A Python transcription returned the inputs for 200,000 random int128 pairs and for the extreme pairs. The hook delta that reaches these functions is a full word chosen by the hook, and both halves are valid int128 values by construction, so no bit pattern is out of range. Evidence: src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-71; src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37; src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Fee fields: LP fee bounds and flag bits, the two 12 bit protocol fee halves, the combined swap fee and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share. Result: MAX_LP_FEE is 1,000,000, which is below 2^20, so a valid fee never touches bit 22 (override flag 0x400000) or bit 23 (dynamic flag 0x800000) (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:15-25). A pool is dynamic only when the fee field equals 0x800000 exactly (LPFeeLibrary.sol:30-32). isValidProtocolFee masks the low and the high 12 bits and compares them with 1001 and 1001 << 12 (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32). I checked the function against the plain rule for one seventh of all 2^24 inputs. calculateSwapFee masks both inputs and returns p + l - floor(p * l / 1e6) (ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). For every p from 0 to 1000 and a grid of l up to 1,000,000 the result stayed at or below 1,000,000 and was at least p and at least l, and it equalled p only when l was 0. The step fee is at least amountIn * swapFee / (1e6 - swapFee) rounded up, or the whole remainder on a partial step (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:72-82, 104), so the protocol share floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * p / 1e6) cannot exceed it and the unchecked subtraction at src/libraries/Pool.sol:391-396 cannot wrap. The Slot0 setter masks the protocol fee to 24 bits before storing it (src/types/Slot0.sol:78-86). Evidence: src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:15-78; src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:8-46; src/libraries/Pool.sol:286-316, 385-397; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:63-105
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Hook return data: which bits of the returned words the PoolManager uses, and whether dirty bits in a hook answer can change a value outside that hook's own pool. Result: parseSelector, parseFee and parseReturnDelta each load one full word at offsets 0x20, 0x60 and 0x40 of the returned bytes (src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:9-28). The selector is compared as bytes4, so only the first four bytes of the first word count (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152). The fee word is used only for a dynamic fee pool and only through an AND with 0x400000, an AND with 0xBFFFFF and a comparison with 1,000,000 (Hooks.sol:263, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, src/libraries/Pool.sol:303-305), so bits above bit 23 are dropped whatever the compiler does with the assembly assignment, and a returned dynamic flag makes the fee fail validation. The delta word is split into two int128 halves and applied with checked arithmetic (Hooks.sol:266-279, 295-313). The hook is credited exactly what the caller is debited (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226). Every value a hook can influence stays inside the pool that names that hook. The length rules are at least 32 bytes for every hook, exactly 64 bytes when a delta is parsed and exactly 96 bytes for beforeSwap (Hooks.sol:152, 166, 259). Evidence: src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:9-28; src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-168, 248-315; src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Hook flag bits and the validity rule: do the 14 flags overlap, does operator precedence give the intended test, and which special addresses pass the rule. Result: The 14 flags are the single bits 13 down to 0 and ALL_HOOK_MASK is 2^14 - 1 (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:27-47). In Solidity the bitwise AND binds tighter than the comparison, so hasPermission tests (address & flag) != 0 and the last line of isValidHookAddress tests (address & mask) > 0 (Hooks.sol:126, 337-339). I enumerated all 16,384 low bit patterns. With a static fee exactly 5,183 are accepted, which is 3^4 * 2^6 - 1: each of the four return delta bits needs its action bit, and the all zero pattern is refused. The zero address is accepted only with a static fee, and an address without flags only with the dynamic fee value (Hooks.sol:124-126). The fixed cases in test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:940-990 agree, including the refusal of an address whose only set bit is bit 14. Low addresses that pass include 0x10, 0x64, 0x100 and 0x101. A precompile or a codeless account at such an address cannot answer with 32 bytes that start with the hook selector, so the hooked action of that pool reverts (Hooks.sol:152-154). That is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and needs victims to choose a pool with that hook address. The identity precompile at 0x04 echoes its input and would pass the selector test, and its address carries bit 2 without bit 6, which the rule refuses (Hooks.sol:112). Evidence: src/libraries/Hooks.sol:27-47, 109-127, 152-154, 337-339; test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:940-990
- all 21 networks, cycle 2. Tick bitmap word and bit positions, the compress function, and the unchecked int24 products in the search for the next initialized tick. Result: position returns the signed tick shifted right by 8 as the word index and the low 8 bits as the bit index (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:35-41). flipTick rejects a tick that is not a multiple of the spacing, divides, and builds the mapping slot from the 256 bit sign extended word index and the mapping slot, which is the encoding Solidity uses for an int16 index (TickBitmap.sol:47-75). For 200,000 random ticks and spacings the assembly compress equalled floor division, and the word index stayed inside int16 (-3466 to 3465 at spacing 1). The lte mask keeps bitPos + 1 low bits and the other mask clears the bits below bitPos (TickBitmap.sol:97, 110). The literal 1 in 1 << bitPos is evaluated as uint256. The largest magnitude the unchecked products can reach is 256 * 32767 = 8,388,352 for word index -1 at the maximum spacing, which is inside int24 (limit 8,388,608), and the swap loop then clamps the result to MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK (src/libraries/Pool.sol:351-356). MAX_TICK_SPACING is int16 max and initialize enforces the range 1 to 32767 (src/libraries/TickMath.sol:26-28, src/PoolManager.sol:119-120). On Ethereum, OP Mainnet, Unichain (the 24,050 byte contract), Ink, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain and Elysium the balance was the same before and after both self transfers and the oversized transfer reverted with an arithmetic panic. A stale read of the receiver balance would have doubled it. The endpoints of Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Arc and HyperEVM do not offer eth_simulateV1 and those of World Chain, Celo and X Layer refused it. On Base, Soneium, Polygon and BNB Smart Chain the log query for a holder was refused, and on Zora and Tempo I found no holder in the log window. Those 14 networks were not tested. This is a test of the deployed code on one path. It does not answer the three leads, which need a compiler. - all 21 networks, cycle 2. Which invariants of flash accounting and custody does the code enforce, and where. This is the list that the other items of this unit try to break. Result: I1, lock. Every function that writes a delta carries onlyWhenUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:96-99 and the modifiers at 147, 189, 258, 291, 300, 305, 310, 322, 332). The flag is set only at line 107, cleared only at line 113, and unlock reverts when it is already set (105). I2, closure. unlock returns only when NonzeroDeltaCount is zero (112). _accountDelta raises the counter when a slot leaves zero and lowers it when a slot returns to zero (368-378), so the counter equals the number of nonzero (account, currency) slots. I3, credits. A positive delta comes from four places only: settle, which adds msg.value when no ERC-20 is synced or the checked rise of balanceOf since sync (349-364); burn, which lowers an ERC-6909 balance by the same amount (332-336, src/ERC6909.sol:85-89); a pool action whose amounts Pool computes (159-183, 206-226, 268-270); and a hook delta that is subtracted from the caller in the same step (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:230, 242, 312). I4, debits. take and mint debit the nominal amount before any external call (294, 326). clear can only bring a positive delta to zero (310-319). I5, custody. The PoolManager sends assets only through Currency.transfer in take (295) and in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56), each after an equal bookkeeping decrease (294 and ProtocolFees.sol:55). I6, one payment bracket. There is one synced currency slot. sync overwrites it (286) or resets it for the native asset (283), an ERC-20 settle resets it (361), and settle rejects msg.value while it is set (356). I7, claims. ERC-6909 balances change only in transfer, transferFrom, _mint and _burn with checked arithmetic (src/ERC6909.sol:25-48, 79-89). From I1 to I7 it follows that for every currency id the PoolManager balance stays at or above pool reserves plus claims plus accrued protocol fees, as long as four properties of the chain and the token hold: T1, balanceOf(PoolManager) of a currency changes only by transfers to or from the PoolManager and by the transferred amount; T2, no second currency id draws on the same balance in another unit; T3, msg.value arrives in full; T4, transient storage is one store per transaction that follows call and revert semantics. The code checks none of T1 to T4. Re-entry into someone else's unlock: a recipient of a native payout, a token with callbacks or a hook gets control while a victim is between its pool action, sync, payment and settle. Can it take the victim's payment, make the victim pay twice, or leave the victim without what it paid for. Result: The victim script is unlock, an action that leaves it owing 1 unit and holding a claim, sync of the currency, payment, settle, return. The attacker may run up to two operations of its own in each of the six gaps, which is more than any real callback allows. Five settings were searched to the end: ERC-20 payment (2,235,193 states, 157 completed runs), native payment (1,211,637 and 130), payment through a one to one native face (1,696,802 and 48), native payment on a chain that has such a face (943,455 and 50), payment through a scaled face (3,811,569 and 393). In every completed run the attacker's wallet did not grow, the victim paid exactly its amount and kept its claim. Runs in which the attacker booked the victim's payment with settleFor, re-synced, or reset the sync with sync(address(0)) all end with a nonzero slot and revert at src/PoolManager.sol:112. A callee can therefore make the surrounding unlock revert, which it could also do by reverting itself, and cannot change who is credited in a transaction that succeeds. - all 21 networks, cycle 2. A stale sync: sync needs no lock, and its two slots are the only settlement state that can outlive an unlock. What can a party gain from a sync left behind inside one transaction, and what would follow if a network failed to wipe transient storage between transactions. Result: unlock ends with the flag false and the counter zero or it reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:105-113), so after any successful call the lock flag and all deltas are zero and only the synced currency and reserves can remain (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32). The model treats a whole sequence as one transaction and found no gain from a sync that survives between unlocks. The effects that remain are these. A later settle with msg.value reverts with NonzeroNativeValue until someone calls sync again (src/PoolManager.sol:356). collectProtocolFees for that ERC-20 reverts (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). The next settle without a new sync credits the caller with every rise of that balance since the stale sync, which inside one transaction can only be the caller's own payment or an inflow it triggered. If a network kept transient storage across transactions, the same reading gives two consequences and no more: native payers who do not call sync first would revert until the slot is reset, and a party could leave a sync in one transaction and book unsolicited inflows, such as a positive rebase, in a later one. Deposits of other users are not exposed, because every ERC-20 settle resets the slot and every payer that follows the interface comment calls sync first (src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:165-171). A leak of the lock flag or of a delta across transactions would be a different and total failure, and the code gives no path to it under call and revert semantics. Each round is sync(face), a forced send of the missing base units, settle, and a native take that restores the remainder, and it turns a native debt of 1 base unit into a credit of 1 face unit, a gain of at most S - 1 base units. With S = 3 the search found a sequence of 7 rounds inside one unlock that took all 13 base units of the toy PoolManager, so the mechanism is real and repeatable. Without forced sends the gain is zero, because settle rejects msg.value while the face is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356), the PoolManager has no receive or fallback function, and the face moves whole units only. The PoolManager would have to be the direct caller, and it can send only transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address), unlockCallback, the IHooks selectors and empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:48-73, 94; src/PoolManager.sol:110; src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-137), which the stablecoin unit found these precompiles reject. Fee collection before a transaction pulls from the fee payer, which is the signer or a sponsor that signed. Custody rule I5 of this unit therefore holds on Tempo apart from issuer roles, which are recorded elsewhere. The source comment says that pulling only from msg.sender is a guideline enforced at each call site and not inside system_transfer_from, so a precompile added to the list later needs the same reading. - all 21 networks, cycle 8. Invariants of flash accounting and custody as this checkout writes them, restated for the opcode focus of this cycle: which instructions each settlement statement depends on, and whether any edge of those instructions can change a credit, a debit, the counter or the lock. Result: The invariants are the seven of cycle 2 (lock, closure, credits, debits, custody, one payment bracket, claims) and the four chain properties T1 to T4, and I found nothing in the current text that changes them. I read src/PoolManager.sol:96-114 and 279-384, src/libraries/Lock.sol:8-27, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-34, CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41, CurrencyReserves.sol:11-38, src/types/Currency.sol:40-118, src/ERC6909.sol:25-89, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59 and src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-70. The settlement path uses few instructions. The delta slot is KECCAK256 of two masked 32 byte words at memory 0 (CurrencyDelta.sol:12-14). The four fixed slots are literals. TLOAD and TSTORE hold the flag, the counter, the deltas and the bracket. The counter moves by ADD and SUB of 1 (NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:21, 31). The delta update is a checked int256 addition (CurrencyDelta.sol:37), so the compiler adds signed comparisons. The credit is a checked subtraction of two balances (PoolManager.sol:360). Every amount passes the cast at SafeCast.sol:56-59, which is a GT style comparison against 2^127. The counter cannot pass below zero: _accountDelta returns on a zero delta (PoolManager.sol:369), it decrements only when next is zero, which means previous was -delta and nonzero, and it increments only when previous is zero (373-377). Every input delta is below 2^127 in size, so the int256 sum at CurrencyDelta.sol:37 would need more than 2^128 calls to overflow. clear compares an int128 with the int256 slot value and can only bring a positive slot to zero (PoolManager.sol:310-319). mint and burn use the masked id currency.toId() for the claim and the truncated currency for the delta, so both sides name the same currency (PoolManager.sol:322-336, Currency.sol:110-118). None of these depends on SAR, SIGNEXTEND, SDIV, SMOD, MULMOD or BYTE. KECCAK256 over 64 bytes, TLOAD, TSTORE, ADD, SUB, AND and the comparisons are in the 185,529 vector battery that OPCODES.md reports clean on all 21 networks. The rollback behaviour of TSTORE inside the PoolManager's own frames is not covered by that battery and is tested in the next item. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:349-378
- all 21 networks, cycle 8. T4 on the deployed PoolManager of each network: after an unlock that fails inside a caller's frame (callback REVERT, callback out of gas, callback INVALID, callback that returns with an open delta), are the lock flag, the nonzero delta counter, the caller's delta slot, the synced currency slot and the caller's ERC-6909 balance back to zero, so that the caller cannot go on to call take, mint or burn without the closure check. Also: does a nested unlock revert, does settle with value revert while an ERC-20 is synced, and does take outside unlock revert. Result: Yes on all 21 networks. A driver placed by code override at an address with no code calls the deployed PoolManager seven times with eth_call; nothing is deployed or sent. In each callback the driver first calls mint(driver, 1, 1), which opens a delta of -1 for currency id 1 and writes a claim. Read from inside the callback before the revert, the lock flag was 1, the counter 1 and the delta slot -1 on every network, so the writes happened. After each failed unlock the driver read all five values through exttload and balanceOf and got zero on every network, for REVERT, for out of gas at 300,000 gas, for INVALID and for a callback that returned with the delta open, which unlock rejected with CurrencyNotSettled (0x5212cba1, src/PoolManager.sol:112). A callback that minted and burned the same amount returned success and left all five values zero. A nested unlock from inside the callback reverted with AlreadyUnlocked (0x5090d6c6, src/PoolManager.sol:105). After sync(0x04) inside the callback the synced currency slot held 0x04, and settle with 1 wei reverted with NonzeroNativeValue (0xb0ec849e, src/PoolManager.sol:356). take(address(0), driver, 0) after all of this reverted with ManagerLocked (0x54e3ca0d, src/PoolManager.sol:96-99). This confirms that inner writes are undone when the outer frame fails and that the lock cannot be left open by a caught failure, on the code path that eth_call uses on each endpoint. Blocks: Ethereum 26484005; Optimism 159956182; Base 61603838; Unichain 64762782; Zora 54408652; Worldchain 38087752; Ink 62012731; Soneium 31188195; Celo 83610382; X Layer 76742107; Arbitrum One 527071731; Robinhood Chain 122108085; Elysium 10268249; Polygon 97870450; BNB Smart Chain 135435881; Avalanche 101243669; Monad 124963667; MegaETH 32714131; Arc 32880504; HyperEVM 52108363; Tempo 50566887. Tempo needed a gas cap of 40,000,000 because a new storage slot costs more there; the result is the same. Unichain runs its own predeploy bytecode and gave the same result. T3 on the deployed PoolManager of each network: does msg.value sent with settle arrive in the PoolManager's balance by the same amount inside the same frame, and does a native take of the same amount restore the balance, so that the credit at src/PoolManager.sol:354 matches a real payment. Result: Yes on all 21 networks. Inside the callback the driver read BALANCE(PoolManager), called settle with 5 base units, read it again, took 5 base units back with take(address(0), driver, 5), read it a third time and reverted. The second reading was the first plus 5 and the third equal to the first on every network, from 0 on Tempo (the driver's balance came from the state override) to about 3.18 * 10^24 on Polygon. The counter was 1 after settle and 0 after take. The PoolManager therefore sees the value as payment in the same unit as SELFBALANCE and BALANCE report it, and the native payout at src/types/Currency.sol:48 moves the stated amount. - Monad, cycle 8. Monad compiles frequently used contracts to x86 code, and eth_call runs the interpreter, so the probe above did not run the compiled path. Do compiled TSTORE and TLOAD keep the same rollback as the interpreter. Result: Yes, by reading the client source on the main branch. The x86 emitter compiles TLOAD and TSTORE to calls of the runtime functions runtime::tload and runtime::tstore (emitter.hpp lines 492-501, dispatched from x86.cpp lines 250-254). The interpreter calls the same runtime::tstore (instruction_table.hpp lines 1357-1375). runtime::tstore exits with an error under a static call and otherwise calls host set_transient_storage, and tload calls get_transient_storage (storage.hpp lines 38-62). The host writes into the current account state of the versioned State object (state.cpp lines 326-329 and 409-413), which is the version stack that the cycle 3 reading found to be popped on a failed frame. Compiled and interpreted code therefore share one transient store and one rollback, and the probe result holds for both. The remaining gap is that I did not confirm that main equals the mainnet release v0.16.5; web3_clientVersion on rpc.monad.xyz returned Monad/unknown. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86/emitter.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/compiler/ir/x86.cpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/interpreter/instruction_table.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/vm/runtime/storage.hpp; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/category-labs/monad/main/category/execution/ethereum/state3/state.cpp
- Polygon, cycle 8. Bor puts two shared caches in front of the interpreter: a cache of KECCAK256 results for 64 byte inputs and a jump destination analysis cache shared by the BlockSTM V2 workers and the prefetcher. Every delta slot (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:12-14), every ERC-6909 balance and allowance slot and every mapping slot of the pools is a 64 byte KECCAK256 input. Can either cache return a wrong slot or a wrong jump answer for the PoolManager. Result: No, as read at tags v2.11.0, v2.11.1 and develop. opKeccak256 uses the cache only when the input is exactly 64 bytes, keys it by the whole 64 bytes copied into an array, and stores a common.Hash value, which Go copies, so the shared hasher buffer cannot alias a stored entry (instructions.go lines 259-290 at v2.11.1, evm.go line 179 for the type of hasherBuf). The cache is a sync.Map with a size cap, and a speculative execution that is later discarded can only leave entries that are true hashes, because the value is a pure function of the key (keccak_cache.go, bounded_cache.go). The jump destination cache is keyed by the code hash as in go-ethereum and stores the bitmap computed from that code (contract.go lines 82-112). A collision in either cache needs a KECCAK256 collision. I could not confirm which bor release the endpoint runs; polygon.drpc.org answers web3_clientVersion with Geth/v10.0.0/drpc. The 64 byte cache is present at all three revisions read. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/instructions.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/keccak_cache.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/bounded_cache.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/contract.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.1/core/vm/evm.go; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.11.0/core/vm/instructions.go
- all 21 networks, cycle 8. Re-entry through the four places where the PoolManager hands control to outside code while settlement state is open: the unlock callback, hooks, the ERC-20 transfer and balanceOf of a currency, and the recipient of a native take. Does any of them run before the PoolManager has written the debit or after it has read a value it then trusts. Result: No ordering gap in the current text. take writes the debit before the transfer (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295). mint writes the debit before the claim (326-327) and burn writes the credit before the burn, and the burn reverts the whole call when the balance or allowance is short (334-335, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22, src/ERC6909.sol:85-89). _settle reads the synced currency, rejects value for an ERC-20, reads the balance, resets the slot and then credits, and the only outside call in it is the balanceOf staticcall, which cannot write state (349-364, src/types/Currency.sol:90-96). sync makes the same staticcall and then writes both slots (279-288). Hooks run inside the pool functions and their deltas are booked after the hook returns (178-183, 221-226, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-160). A re-entering party shares the lock but not the caller's delta slots, which are keyed by msg.sender (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-16), and unlock returns only when every slot of every party is zero (src/PoolManager.sol:112). The cycle 2 victim and two account searches cover the sequences; this item confirms that the text they model has not changed in the lines they cite. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:291-336

I compared them by reading. A diff command on the two files was refused by the session's permission layer, so the comparison is by reading only. Result: The eight tests hold: a delegatecall into modifyLiquidity, swap or donate of the real manager passes the lock check in the proxy's context and then fails with DelegateCallNotAllowed, because the modifier order is onlyWhenUnlocked then noDelegateCall (src/PoolManager.sol:147-148, 189-190, 258-259, src/NoDelegateCall.sol:24-32). The proxy double differs from the production contract in three places. It puts noDelegateCall on its own unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn (ProxyPoolManager.sol:58, 151, 156, 163, 176, 181), while the production functions carry only the lock check (PoolManager.sol:104, 291, 300, 305, 322, 332). It emits Initialize after afterInitialize (ProxyPoolManager.sol:90-94), while production emits before (PoolManager.sol:139-141). Its sync is public. The proxy forwards take, settle, mint, burn and clear by delegatecall and expects them to run, so the double is consistent with production functions that accept delegatecall. I checked whether the missing modifier matters for funds. A delegatecall runs PoolManager code against the storage, transient storage and balance of the calling contract. The lock flag, the deltas, the claims and every transfer then belong to that contract. Nothing held by the PoolManager can be reached this way. The same holds for an account that points an EIP-7702 delegation at the PoolManager, because the delegated code runs in the context of that account. EIP-7702 says that CALL loads the code at the delegated address and executes it in the context of the authority, and EIP-7 says that the call created by DELEGATECALL has the same sender and value as the original call. I fetched both texts in this session. I did not test how the client of each network implements DELEGATECALL and delegation, so for the 20 networks other than Ethereum this rests on the two specifications. ProtocolFeesImplementation mirrors ProtocolFees without change and adds a lock toggle that nothing reads.
