Result: No token keeps a count or a volume of transfers per sender, a cooldown or a last transfer block for the PoolManager that a repaid take can use up. Coverage: Ethereum 304 tokens (304 traced, blocks 26475322 to 26475361); Optimism 108 tokens (108 traced, blocks 159903969 to 159904258); Base 253 tokens (248 traced, blocks 61081750 to 61081750); Unichain 34 tokens (34 traced, blocks 64658362 to 64658362); X Layer 107 tokens (107 traced, blocks 76637685 to 76638664); Arbitrum One 195 tokens (195 traced, blocks 526700807 to 526701162); Robinhood Chain 201 tokens (201 traced, blocks 121133905 to 121139717); Elysium 300 tokens (300 traced, blocks 9752024 to 9752024); Polygon 262 tokens (262 traced, blocks 97800833 to 97801219); BNB Smart Chain 39 tokens (39 traced, blocks 135204514 to 135208099); Avalanche 75 tokens (75 traced, blocks 101130625 to 101130625); Monad 111 tokens (111 traced, blocks 124619495 to 124619495); MegaETH 67 tokens (67 traced, blocks 32609710 to 32610811); Tempo 73 tokens (73 traced, blocks 50372931 to 50374937); HyperEVM 262 tokens (262 traced, blocks 52002201 to 52003492); Ink 94 tokens (94 traced, blocks 61908538 to 61909282). The round trip left no storage change for 2,302 of 2,480 traced tokens. For the rest the changes are of these kinds, none of which can make a later take or payment fail: balance checkpoints that add one entry per block (FXS, LDO, RHUB, PACDAO, PEAK); Aave style tokens, where a full transfer clears the collateral flag of the PoolManager in the Aave pool and updates incentive indexes, with no effect for an account without debt; Compound v3, Pendle, Radiant, Neverland, Benqi and DeltaPrime reward or index updates; rebasing tokens with rounding of one base unit; the deposit timestamp of the PoolManager in the Hop swap contract; the USDG timestamp on X Layer (see finding); holder lists and reward trackers that change for the recipient only. I retested 40 tokens of these kinds with 25 consecutive round trips in one call. 39 succeeded with the final balance equal to the starting balance. The call for uPEG on Ethereum, an ERC-404 style token, ran out of a 45 million gas allowance and gave no result. The one way diff differed from the plain pattern of two balance slots for 111 of 2,281 tokens: storage credit slots on Tempo, holder counts, dividend corrections, reward trackers and tokens that refused the transfer. The only one that enforces a limit is ViciCoin on Polygon (see finding). Tokens that refuse a transfer from the PoolManager are listed in a separate item. Securitize wrappers on X Layer (v4CRCL, v4MSTR, v4COIN, v4HOOD, v4VOLOROST2) and the multiplier tokens BMNRx and ANTx: does a payout from the PoolManager count against a limit of the wrapper or of the Securitize token behind it. Result: No limit found. The wrappers expose allow list, hook list and wrapper list functions and no limit or rate function. A payout from the PoolManager to an address that the wrapper permits burns the wrapper token and moves the Securitize token from the wrapper to the recipient. In the traced payout of half the v4MSTR balance to 0x10b5b66491d8f91310a85b49cf7a15ef6bbc936a the wrapper wrote its total supply and the PoolManager balance, the Securitize token wrote four balance words, and the compliance contract 0x2fc11ad109c41ab1d347d45d32a31eb3d09e66f6 was called and wrote nothing. A payout of the full balance also updates the wallet list of the Securitize token. Transfers to addresses outside the allow list revert with TRANSFER_FAILED, so an account without Securitize onboarding cannot do the round trip at all. BMNRx and ANTx had a clean round trip diff. The PoolManager is opted out at initialisation and cannot change that, so the rule binds the recipient of one transfer and a smaller take or an opted out recipient passes. - Tempo, cycle 4. Tempo storage credits (TIP-1060): the PoolManager has one credit balance at 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 that every user of the PoolManager shares. Can an ordinary account use it up, and what does the next user lose. Result: Gas only. Clearing a PoolManager slot mints one credit for the PoolManager account, and the clearing refund of EIP-3529 is zero on Tempo. Creating a PoolManager slot costs 245,000 gas more unless a credit is available, in which case the sender of that transaction gets the amount back at the end of the transaction. balanceOf(PoolManager) at the precompile returned 13 at block 50,377,344. Any account can spend these credits by creating slots it pays 5,000 gas for, such as ERC-6909 balances of one base unit under fresh ids (src/PoolManager.sol:322-328). A liquidity provider who clears slots when leaving gets no refund, and the next creator of a slot gets the benefit or pays the full price. No call fails and no balance moves. The same counter exists per token: a transfer to a new holder used one credit of stcUSD (2 to 1) in my trace and a round trip restored it. Evidence: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tempoxyz/tempo/main/tips/tip-1060.md; https://github.com/tempoxyz/tempo/releases/tag/v1.10.1 (TIP-1060 listed in the T7 upgrade); rpc eth_call balanceOf and eth_getStorageAt on 0x1060000000000000000000000000000000000000 and debug_traceCall on https://rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz at block 50,377,344, client tempo/v1.19.0-697ea97
- Tempo, MegaETH, Monad, cycle 4. Network rules that could throttle the PoolManager address after another account used it: TIP-403 policies on Tempo, resource limits on MegaETH, the reserve balance on Monad. Result: None of them keeps state per called contract. A TIP-403 policy is a white list, a black list or a compound of three such lists, and isAuthorized is a view that reads set membership. It holds no amount, count or time, and only the policy admin changes it. MegaETH enforces compute gas, data size, KV update and state growth limits per transaction and per block and has no limit per account. The block limit on state growth is covered by F-042. The Monad reserve balance applies to externally owned accounts that pay gas, as an earlier cycle confirmed in the client source. Evidence: https://tempo.com/developers/docs/protocol/tip403/spec; https://docs.megaeth.com/spec/megaevm/resource-limits; https://docs.monad.xyz/developer-essentials/reserve-balance
- all 21 networks, cycle 4. Rate limited bridged tokens: do xERC20 limits, OFT rate limits, CCTP limits or Superchain token bridge limits sit on the plain transfer path that take uses. Result: No case found. In every bridged token I traced, a transfer between two holders changed two balance slots only. That includes USDT0 on Ink, Unichain, X Layer, MegaETH, HyperEVM and Tempo, USDC and bridged USDC.e and WBTC on the trace networks where the PoolManager holds them, and the Paxos tokens. AGL is an OFT whose limit of 1.8e19 AGL per send sits in the send path, and its transfer path was read in source. Bridge limits are read in mint, burn and send functions, which the PoolManager never calls (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75 calls transfer only). On the five networks without a trace endpoint this rests on the 25 round test. - Optimism, Base, Unichain, Zora, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc, HyperEVM, cycle 5. Method: code of every currency with a balance was grouped by selector set (own code plus implementation behind the usual proxy slots), every function with a name that suggests locking, vesting, staking, granting, minting, distributing, claiming, burning or transferring was called by an ordinary account that had just received a third of the PoolManager balance, with the PoolManager as address argument, and a stub at the PoolManager address then tried to send out the full balance and the balance minus the amount. Coverage: Optimism 1594 tokens, 403 families, 7242 trials; Base 9108 tokens, 594 families, 10487 trials; Unichain 4562 tokens, 247 families, 2830 trials; Zora 41 tokens, 18 families, 302 trials; Worldchain 851 tokens, 271 families, 3600 trials; Ink 3438 tokens, 184 families, 2794 trials; Soneium 70 tokens, 53 families, 806 trials; Celo 92 tokens, 43 families, 700 trials; X Layer 96 tokens, 27 families, 512 trials; Arbitrum One 5502 tokens, 1188 families, 20591 trials; Robinhood Chain 738773 tokens, 7616 families, 80866 trials; Elysium 129491 tokens, 577 families, 6606 trials; Avalanche 1841 tokens, 521 families, 9100 trials; Monad 8375 tokens, 405 families, 6452 trials; MegaETH 67 tokens, 32 families, 559 trials; Tempo 73 tokens, 19 families, 237 trials; Arc 261204 tokens, 1143 families, 11682 trials; HyperEVM 262 tokens, 68 families, 934 trials. - Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Arbitrum One, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, cycle 5. Part three: public triggers of a rebase on pooled tokens beyond the named ones. For 114 tokens with rebasing indicators on eleven networks (rebase, gonsForBalance, stakingContract with index, monetaryPolicy, rebaseOptIn, rewardMultiplier) the related contracts were read from public getters, and every function with at most two simple arguments on them was called by an ordinary account while the PoolManager balance was measured. Result: The staking rebase is open to any caller on sVALUES 0x8d8b9044662644e2502e4a6747846f6b0fdaf0bd on Polygon (1,133.70 pooled), on sOHM 0x04906695d6d12cf5459975d7c3c03356e4ccd460 (249.39 pooled), the older sOHM 0x04f2694c8fcee23e8fd0dfea1d4f5bb8c352111f (12.37) and sVEC 0x66d5c66e7c83e0682d947176534242c9f19b3365 (135.07) on Ethereum, and on sT 0x14194a883fc79af1180a9294dff9e6e8d8933330 on Arbitrum One (dust). The fourth word of epoch() is zero for all five, so the next rebase distributes nothing and nothing can be booked today. They join the class of the Polygon finding if distribution resumes. Of the named tokens, sKLIMA would rise by 851,020 base units and sNVB by 54,992,087 base units at the time of the test, and sLGNS, sATH and sSAC were not due. On the vaults of OUSD, OETH, their Base counterpart and Sperax USDs no call changed the PoolManager balance, which fits contracts being outside the rebase unless they opt in. Two Ethereum tokens named Ti have an owner contract with a public poke() that raised the calling account's balance and left the PoolManager balance unchanged. A trigger that needs more than two arguments or a contract two steps away from the token is not covered. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-assigned-balance.work/hop.py:1
- Ethereum, Optimism, Unichain, Worldchain, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Polygon, Monad, Arc, HyperEVM, cycle 5. Tokens where a call by an ordinary account raised the PoolManager balance at no cost to the caller (class free raise in the trial sweep). Result: Apart from TITHE these are tokens with a mint function open to any caller, mostly test tokens: 27 on Ethereum, 20 on Polygon, 19 on Robinhood Chain, 16 on Arbitrum One, 12 on Unichain, 5 each on Monad and Arc, 2 each on Optimism, World Chain and Elysium, 1 on HyperEVM. None has a price at coins.llama.fi. A token that anyone can mint has no value to take, and a credit obtained with freshly minted units is a claim on that token only (src/PoolManager.sol:364 accounts per currency). Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-assigned-balance.work/raw/summary.json:1

- Base, Tempo, Arc, cycle 5. Network native token standards: do B20 tokens on Base, TIP-20 tokens on Tempo or the USDC token of Arc count amounts in balanceOf that the holder cannot transfer, and can a third party assign such amounts. Result: No evidence of it. The B20 introduction describes an ERC-20 superset with roles, per feature pause, policies, mint, burn and seize, and names no held, locked or vesting balance. The full balance transfer from the PoolManager address succeeded for the B20 token OUSD on Base (5.33 million pooled), for 72 of 73 Tempo currencies (the exception is the token frozen by its issuer, already recorded) and for USDC on Arc. Earlier cycles listed every balance write of the TIP-20 precompile and found none that a third party can direct at the PoolManager. I did not read B20 or Arc node source for this question in this cycle. Evidence: https://docs.base.org/specifications/b20/introduction

## Reading of the source (theme-claim-operators)

- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Reading of the claim transfer and burn checks in this repository: src/ERC6909.sol:35-48 (transferFrom), src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22 (_burnFrom), src/PoolManager.sol:322-336 (mint and burn), src/types/Currency.sol:110-118 (toId and fromId), src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59. Result: transferFrom skips the allowance step only when msg.sender is the sender or isOperator[sender][msg.sender] is true. Otherwise it reads allowance[sender][msg.sender][id] and writes allowed - amount with checked arithmetic unless the allowance is the maximum uint256, so a spender without enough allowance reverts. The balance of the sender is reduced with checked arithmetic. _burnFrom applies the same test with from in place of sender and then calls _burn. PoolManager.burn credits the delta of msg.sender and burns from the named account, so an operator or spender receives the value of what it burns. That is the intended meaning of an approval. mint and burn truncate the id to 160 bits before use and transfer, transferFrom and approve use the full 256 bit id, so an id with high bits set can be held and approved and can never be burned. That strands only the holder's own claim. An operator right covers every id and both transferFrom and burn and has no expiry. I found no way in this code for an account without an approval to move another account's claims on any network. Evidence: src/ERC6909.sol:36

- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Do the shared contracts that run command lists or batches for any caller hold an approval? I matched every operator and spender address of all 21 networks against Multicall3, Multicall2, Permit2, the Across MulticallHandler, the 1inch v6 router, the 0x exchange proxy and AllowanceHolder, the CoW settlement contract, the three ERC-4337 EntryPoint versions, the Safe MultiSend contracts, the LiFi diamond, the Kyber meta router, CreateX and every Uniswap contract listed in networks.json. Result: Six kinds of match, all without effect today. (1) The Universal Router is operator of owner 0xd7c7200e8d781013e16db8418ded4767a5beb598 on Robinhood Chain (0x8876789976decbfcbbbe364623c63652db8c0904) and holds allowances from three owners on Base (0x6ff5693b99212da76ad316178a184ab56d299b43, ids USDC, 0x2105 and 0). Its verified source rejects every v4 action other than swaps, SETTLE_ALL, TAKE_ALL, SETTLE, TAKE and TAKE_PORTION with UnsupportedAction (V4Router.sol:34-82 on Robinhood Chain, line 78 on Base) and its Dispatcher makes low level calls only to Permit2, the v3 position manager, the v4 PositionManager, itself and poolManager.initialize. Its token payments use the ERC-20 selectors, which the PoolManager does not have. Its bytecode has no constant for burn (0xf5298aca) or the ERC-6909 transferFrom (0xfe99049a), also in the shifted form the optimizer writes. (2) The PositionManager is operator of one owner on Base and spender for one id on BNB Smart Chain and on Robinhood Chain. It refuses actions 0x17 and 0x18 and has neither constant. (3) Permit2 is spender for one owner on Base and one on BNB Smart Chain. It calls transferFrom(address,address,uint256) with selector 0x23b872dd, which the PoolManager does not have. (4) The PoolManager itself is spender or operator for seven owners on Ethereum, Base, Unichain, Robinhood Chain, Monad and Elysium. It never calls itself. (5) The zero address is operator of one account on BNB Smart Chain and spender on Robinhood Chain, and the native token contract 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 is operator of one account on Polygon. None of these owners holds a claim, and the token contract makes only value transfers. (6) No Multicall, EntryPoint, bridge handler, aggregator or settlement contract of the list appears on any network. These approvals stay safe only while the approved code has no path to burn or transferFrom. The Actions library already reserves BURN_6909, so a later router that handles it with a payer chosen by the caller would make the existing approvals usable by anyone. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/0x8876789976decbfcbbbe364623c63652db8c0904?fields=sources,compilation and https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/8453/0x6ff5693b99212da76ad316178a184ab56d299b43?fields=sources,compilation; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/raw/triage_8453.json, triage_4663.json, triage_56.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Call shape probe with a positive control. From an unrelated account, each approved contract whose owners hold claims was sent 25 shapes that wrap PoolManager.transferFrom(owner, receiver, id, amount): the four Multicall3 functions, execute, executeBatch, call, forward, exec, multicall, functionCall, invoke, the ERC-7821 and ERC-7579 execute modes, Safe multiSend and the inner calldata sent raw. Each shape ran with amount 1 and with amount balance plus 1, and a shape counts when the first succeeds and the second does not. Result: 489 contracts on 16 networks, no positive. Control on Ethereum: with a state override that makes Multicall3 an operator of a claim holder the probe reports aggregate, aggregate3, tryAggregate and aggregate3Value as positive, and without the override it reports none. Evidence: https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_call with stateDiff override; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/probe.py and raw/probe_<chainId>.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Caller test of unlockCallback. For each of 714 approved contracts the same calldata was sent once with from set to the PoolManager and once from an unrelated account, with five payloads. A contract whose callback has no caller check can be driven by any account that has unlocked the PoolManager itself. Result: 309 contracts have an unlockCallback. 292 answer the two callers differently. 17 answer alike and were looked at one by one: 12 revert with the same custom error for both callers before any call to the PoolManager and their owners hold no claims or the trace reached nothing, 2 are the tx.origin bound contracts described for Ethereum and Arc, 2 are test contracts on Robinhood Chain whose callback returns without a caller check, which have no burn or transferFrom constant and whose owners hold no claims, and 1 on BNB Smart Chain has no burn or transferFrom constant. Limit: the test looks for the callback selector in the code at the approved address or at its EIP-7702 delegate. The 264 clone proxies (Bunni tokens and Panoptic collateral trackers) were therefore covered through their verified implementations, which check the caller at BunniToken.sol:255-258, CollateralTracker.sol:352-353 and SemiFungiblePositionManager.sol:520-521. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/guard.py and raw/guard_<chainId>.json
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Ink, Celo, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, HyperEVM, cycle 5. Reach test with debug_traceCall. For 201 code groups of approved contracts (one representative per implementation, chosen by exposure) every dispatcher selector was called from an unrelated account with six argument fillings that place an approving owner, a claim id of that owner, the caller and small numbers in the argument words: 5,388 selectors and about 32,000 traces. The call tree was searched for calls to the PoolManager and the first argument of each burn and transferFrom was compared with the caller, the contract and the approving owner. Result: 50 contracts have a selector that reaches the PoolManager from an unrelated account. In every burn or transferFrom seen, the debited account is the caller or the contract itself, with one exception that pays the debited owner (redeemFees on Robinhood Chain, see that entry). 33 traces failed at the endpoint. Five approved addresses are 677 byte proxies with a private implementation slot (Ethereum, OP Mainnet, Unichain, Base, Robinhood Chain, one owner each, 4 to 84 USD of claims). The main run saw only their two proxy functions, so I traced the selectors of the implementation through the proxy on Ethereum, OP Mainnet and Unichain (5,350 and 8,926 bytes, with owner and authorized lists) and nothing reached the PoolManager. The Base and Robinhood Chain copies were not finished. This test shows what happened for the fillings I used. A function that needs a well formed struct or a signature before it reaches unlock shows up as not reaching, so the test supports the answer no and does not prove it for unverified code. Evidence: https://eth.drpc.org, https://base.api.pocket.network, https://unichain.drpc.org, https://arbitrum.drpc.org, https://robinhood.drpc.org, https://polygon.drpc.org, https://avalanche.drpc.org, https://hyperliquid.drpc.org, https://rpc.monad.xyz, https://bsc.api.pocket.network, https://rpc-qnd.inkonchain.com, https://op.api.pocket.network, https://celo.api.pocket.network debug_traceCall; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/reach.py, raw/reach_<chainId>.json and raw/reach_proxy677.txt
- Ethereum, Base, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, Robinhood Chain, cycle 5. EIP-7702 delegated accounts among the approved addresses. Code 0xef0100 followed by a delegate address was found at 56 approved addresses: 47 on Ethereum (all delegate to 0xb0c75276657e80ff04c98a3809dfc39a409a8736 and all are operators of the one account 0x82ccba35ad0c7a62230ef8ff337ac67f4cce0ea5, itself a delegated account with claims of about 740 USD), 3 on Robinhood Chain, 2 on Polygon, 2 on Base, 1 on BNB Smart Chain and 1 on Monad. The delegates are 0x63c0c19a282a1b52b07dd5a65b58948a07dae32b, 0x612373d7003d694220f7800eeaf8e3924c0951d3, 0x7702cb554e6bfb442cb743a7df23154544a7176c, 0x69007702764179f14f51cdce752f4f775d74e139 and 0x1c08930b2d330447e6c05b5be8c4caf172b4a174. Result: No public batch function was found. The 47 accounts on Ethereum were part of the call shape probe. For the nine delegated accounts on the other five networks I sent the 25 execute and batch shapes from an unrelated account with one inner call that must succeed and one that must fail: eight accounts revert on every shape and the ninth returns the same data for both, so none executes the inner call. The delegate 0xb0c75276 dispatches on msg.sender: the PoolManager, the account itself, or an address stored in transient slot 0 by the account's own flow. One handler (selector 0x10d1e85c) runs without that stored address and makes the account call PoolManager.take(currency, msg.sender, amount) with values from calldata for any caller. Inside another account's unlock this pays the caller and leaves the delegated account with a negative delta that only a payment through settleFor or the account's own actions can clear (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 305-307), so the caller gains nothing from this handler alone. I did not decompile the rest of the 24,384 byte delegate. The right of a delegated operator follows whatever code its signer delegates to next (assumption A7). Evidence: https://eth.drpc.org debug_traceCall of 0x04f9af14b8d9eccd220c91109a1f3b5e608f713e with selector 0x10d1e85c, https://ethereum-rpc.publicnode.com eth_getCode; research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/raw/triage_1.json, raw/reach_1.json, raw/probe_delegated.json
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Does any approved operator or spender sit at an address that a network lets other parties use as msg.sender: system addresses, predeploys in the 0x4200 range, precompiles, alias addresses of L1 senders, the HyperEVM system addresses, Tempo and Arc precompile ranges?. Result: No. Apart from the zero address, address 0x01 (set and removed on Robinhood Chain) and the Polygon native token contract listed above, every operator and spender is an ordinary contract or account. No claim approval on any of the 21 networks depends on who can produce a call from a system address. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-claim-operators.work/raw/logs_<chainId>.json and raw/state_<chainId>.json

- Ethereum, cycle 5. FeeHookV3 at 0x0d62529346ac2c61f5c0582210d01214687bc0cc (5,116 pools, no initialize flag, both return delta flags, 5.31 ETH held): can a pool created by a stranger move the ETH that the hook owes to creators and partners?. Result: No. The hook has no initialize callback, so any PoolKey can be initialized. beforeSwap reverts unless currency0 is native (FeeHookV3.sol, PoolMustHaveEthAsCurrency0). Every fee credited in ethOwed is taken from the PoolManager in the same callback (poolManager.take of the same amount that is returned as the hook delta), and claim() pays only ethOwed[msg.sender]. Fee settings are stored per token, and only the address returned by token.factory() may register a creator, a recipient list, a partner or a custom fee for that token. A stranger's pool therefore adds real ETH that the stranger's swappers paid and cannot debit another token. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x0d62529346ac2c61f5c0582210d01214687bc0cc
- Ethereum, cycle 5. UniversalKlikHook at 0x96b893683afbfec071e90f78d00de4bb932fe0cc (2,240 pools) and 0x07f17023db9cec3f8c6bb53c6940e29dffb0a0cc (1,290 pools): beforeInitialize accepts every caller. Does the hook keep state or funds that a foreign pool can reach?. Result: No. beforeInitialize only stores block.number under the pool id, and a second initialize of the same id reverts in the PoolManager, which undoes the write. The swap callbacks take the fee in ETH from the PoolManager and forward it in the same call to the platform treasury and to the token address. The hook keeps no ledger and both addresses hold no ETH, tokens or claims. This is an older Klik hook (VERSION 2) without the pending fee ledger of the finding. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x96b893683afbfec071e90f78d00de4bb932fe0cc
- Unichain, cycle 5. UniMemeHook 0xb4960cd4f9147f9e37a7aa9005df7156f61e4444 (777 pools) and UniderpHook 0xcc2efb167503f2d7df0eae906600066aec9e8444 (114 pools), no initialize flag, afterSwap return delta: the referral ledger is per account, with no pool id. Can a stranger's pool or a stranger's hookData set the referrer of a token creator and collect or block that token's fees?. Result: No. The verified UniMemeReferral source writes referrerOf[creator] from hookData, where creator comes from a call to the pool currency. The deployed referral proxy 0x3622415b9fcb69b4395d1ad152ea002309c34fed behaves differently: in an eth_simulateV1 run of afterAddLiquidity from the PoolManager address with a referrer in hookData, the RefferalInfo event names the simulated sender (the PoolManager address, which was both the transaction origin and the caller of the hook) as invitee, and referrerOf(creator) stays zero. A swapper therefore cannot write the referrer of a token creator through hookData. In afterSwap the sum of the take calls equals the returned delta in each of the four possible referral tree shapes, and referrerOf[address(0)] cannot be written, so the mismatch case in distributeReferralFee cannot be reached. Both hooks hold no claims or balances. A token contract that reverts on receiving native currency in creator() position blocks exact input sells of its own pool only, which is a pool creator matter. Evidence: https://unichain.blockscout.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/0xb4960cd4f9147f9e37a7aa9005df7156f61e4444 and https://mainnet.unichain.org (eth_simulateV1 at block 64,676,429)
- Ethereum, Base, Unichain, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, cycle 5. Clanker hooks (ClankerHookStaticFeeV2, ClankerHookStaticFee, ClankerHookDynamicFee; 0x6c24d0bc... on Ethereum, 0xb429d62f... on Base, 0xbc6e5abd... on Unichain, 0xf7ac6695... and 0xfd213be7... on Arbitrum One, 0x48b8f6ad... on Robinhood Chain, 0xc5d30902... on BNB Smart Chain, 0x94f802a9... on Monad): they hold ERC-6909 claims and offer initializePoolOpen to every caller. Can a pool opened by a stranger take those claims?. Result: No. A direct PoolManager.initialize always reverts with UnsupportedInitializePath (ClankerHookV2.sol line 581). The hook creates pools itself through initializePool (factory only) and initializePoolOpen (any caller, any two tokens), and the PoolManager skips the callback when the hook is the caller (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:171-175). All per pool state (locker, mevModule, poolExtension, clankerIsToken0, poolCreationTimestamp) is stored under the pool id. The protocol fee is minted as claims in the paired currency, and _hookFeeClaim burns the whole claim balance of that currency and sends it to the immutable factory (lines 413 to 432). A stranger's pool can only trigger that sweep to the factory earlier. Read in the Robinhood Chain source. The other addresses returned the same errors in the probe and were not read line by line. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/0x48b8f6ad3a1b4aa477314c9a23035b8f84dde8cc
- Robinhood Chain, Base, Arc, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, cycle 5. Doppler initializer hooks (DopplerHookInitializer 0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544 with 244,744 pools on Robinhood Chain, 0xf0d631d54c7e1040ccfa1c2ed737973d6a652544 on Arc and BNB Smart Chain, 0xbdf938149ac6a781f94faa0ed45e6a0e984c6544 and DecayMulticurveInitializerHook 0xbb7784a4d481184283ed89619a3e3ed143e1adc0 on Base, 0x580ca49389d83b019d07e17e99454f2f218e2dc0 on Monad): the hook owns the positions of every pool and holds collected fees. Can a pool from a stranger reach them?. Result: No. _beforeInitialize requires sender == address(this) (DopplerHookInitializer.sol line 497), and the PoolManager does not call the hook when the hook itself initializes, so only the hook's own initialize function, which is limited to the Airlock, creates pools. afterSwap looks the pool id up in getAsset and does nothing for an unknown id. FeesManager stores cumulated fees, shares and the PoolKey per pool id and pays a beneficiary only from fees that _collectFees returned for that pool. Read in the Robinhood Chain source. The other four addresses reject an ordinary initializer with the same OnlyInitializer error. Pools that an ordinary account creates through the Airlock with a quote currency of its choice were not examined. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/4663/0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544
- Ink, cycle 5. AegisHook 0xe449e013004db4a5681e9622ca10c5ba0ea610cc (102 pools): afterInitialize accepts any caller when the fee is dynamic, and the hook mints ERC-6909 claims for its fee and burns them when it reinvests. Can a foreign pool spend claims that belong to another pool?. Result: Not through the hook. The fee share hookFeePpm is zero for a pool until the owner sets it, so a foreign pool charges no hook fee. Pending fees, the per swap fee cache, the runtime data and the reinvest cooldown are stored per pool id, and _tryReinvest burns at most the pending amount of the pool that is swapping. The engine, the oracle manager, the dynamic fee manager and the limit order manager that the hook calls with the foreign PoolKey were not read. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/57073/0xe449e013004db4a5681e9622ca10c5ba0ea610cc
- Zora, cycle 5. StrategyHookV2 hooks on Zora (0x1f141a2f..., 0x7ae8de96... and two unverified addresses with the same flags, one pool each): initialize succeeds for a second pool with the same currency pair. What can that pool do?. Result: Nothing after launch. beforeInitialize only checks that currency1 is the strategy token. beforeAddLiquidity allows one deposit per hook, tracked in a single flag, so a second pool cannot receive liquidity once the real pool has it, and a swap without liquidity moves nothing and produces no fee. Before the first deposit an account could use the one allowed deposit on its own pool and block the launch, which concerns the deployer only. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/7777777/0x1f141a2f4eb256c58a6e008885c6fdc966576844
- Optimism, Polygon, Celo, Arbitrum One, Avalanche, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, Soneium, Worldchain, MegaETH, Ethereum, cycle 5. Hooks with flags beforeSwap and beforeSwapReturnDelta only (addresses ending in 8088, for example 0xf0e1b03731fa1c94b30e90a9a61368e2f5968088 on Optimism, 0x1743c5352f4e11aadb8a6023a10499703b600088 on Polygon, 0x8ca169714fc17174e5c6ef29bf2833f9bdb1c088 on BNB Smart Chain) and the variant with afterInitialize (0x987105e9... on Optimism, 0xc9987661... on Polygon, 0x89fcd097... on Arbitrum One, 0x8d92ff0a... on Monad): initialize is open. Does a pool from a stranger get served?. Result: The first group answers beforeSwap with PoolNotRegistered, InvalidPoolKey or HookPaused for a pool it did not register. The Optimism hook reports version UniswapV2LPHook v1.1.1, stores a Uniswap V2 pair per pool id, and its registration, setPoolFee, setPaused and execute functions revert with OnlyOwner for an ordinary caller. Existing pools were registered by the owner 0x2a315c59a6a95aeeec085c73badac801c2f4209f in a call to the hook. The variant with afterInitialize pairs an ERC-4626 vault with its asset. Its afterInitialize registers any pool whose pair passes the vault check: in an eth_simulateV1 run on Polygon an ordinary account initialized a second pool for USDC and waUSDC, getPoolCount rose from 89 to 90 and pools(id) of the new pool equals that of the existing one. A stranger can therefore register a pool for a vault contract it wrote. None of these hooks holds claims, tokens or native currency between transactions, except 0x60451c7c... on Polygon and 0x92385e5b... on MegaETH, which hold token balances and reject a foreign PoolKey with InvalidPoolKey. No path to funds of other pools was found. The owner's execute function can make the hook call any address, which is an owner power. Evidence: https://mainnet.optimism.io and https://polygon.drpc.org (eth_call and eth_simulateV1, 23 November 2026)
- Arc, cycle 5. Arc hook 0x4ab0bf61327761fffc5910052d9e0b9a94f960cc (1,260 pools, unverified, holds 35.4 units of native claims, selectors owed(address,address), claim(address), poolConfig(bytes32)): initialize succeeds for a second pool of a factory token with another tick spacing. Can that pool reach the claims?. Result: No path found. beforeInitialize rejects tokens that the token factory did not create (NotFactoryToken). In an eth_simulateV1 run the second pool was initialized, poolConfig(new id) still reverted with PoolNotConfigured, poolConfig of the real pool was unchanged, and beforeSwap for the new pool reverted with PoolNotConfigured, so the pool cannot be swapped. The hook has no liquidity callbacks. The configuration function 0x7e19851a rejects an ordinary caller and the token factory with OnlyStrategy(address). Who the strategy is was not established. Evidence: https://arc.drpc.org (eth_simulateV1) and https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io (eth_call), 23 November 2026
- MegaETH, cycle 5. HOMIEHook 0xeecbbd7ceb246684b8f621dc9dddca8f72b200c4 on MegaETH (3 pools, no initialize flag, afterSwap return delta). Result: The fee logic runs only for pool ids that the owner registered with registerPool, which requires the HOMIE token as one currency. afterSwap returns zero for any other pool. The hook holds nothing. Evidence: https://megaeth.blockscout.com/api/v2/smart-contracts/0xeecbbd7ceb246684b8f621dc9dddca8f72b200c4
- all 21 networks, cycle 5. Across the 111 hooks probed on the 21 networks: is there a hook with a return delta flag that accepts initialize from an ordinary account for arbitrary currencies and then returns a non zero delta, or calls take, mint, burn or settle, for that pool?. Result: Three groups do. FeeHookV3 and UniversalKlikHook on Ethereum and UniMemeHook, UniderpHook and hook 0x782d2a5624cfac246fd8f001ccd4d7582a0b8444 on Unichain charge their fee on any pool and pay it out or credit it in the same callback from the amount they take, which is covered above (0x782d2a56... is unverified and was judged from its probe result only). OmniHook 0x03f4051e621ee3f3652adef2c453458a777e40cc on World Chain (14 pools) does the same: it takes its fee to itself and credits five fixed recipients in owed[currency][recipient], so the ledger is per currency and each entry is backed by tokens taken in that currency. The Klik fee hooks are the third group and are the finding. Every other probed hook with a return delta flag either rejects the stranger's initialize or reverts or returns zero for a pool it does not know. A callback that reverted with ManagerLocked in the direct call shows that the hook tried a PoolManager call that needs an unlocked manager, which is how fee taking hooks were recognised. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/005/theme-shared-hooks.work/raw/probe: one JSON file per chain and hook with the eth_call results

## Reading of the source (loose-guards)

- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Lead L-313, first item: collectProtocolFees never reads the lock and skips the synced check for address(0) (src/ProtocolFees.sol:48-52 against src/interfaces/IProtocolFees.sol:40). Result: Answered in cycle 1 and not repeated: the cleared items for chain ids 1, 137, 56 and 5042 walked a native collection while a native face is synced and found that it lowers the settler own credit, and the critic of cycle 5 confirmed on Ethereum, Polygon and Arc that the deployed contracts collect inside an unlock. This unit added one read. The fee controllers of the eight networks that have one (chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 42161, 4663, 137, 56 and 5042) all expose the same sixteen selectors, among them 0xe0511234 for collect((address,uint256)[]) and 0x06ab95ba for triggerFeeUpdate with a PoolKey argument, and each answers POOL_MANAGER() with the PoolManager of its network and TOKEN_JAR() with one fixed address. Seven of them are 4,544 bytes long and the one on Arc is 3,480 bytes. I did not read the adapter code on the seven networks other than Ethereum, so that the recipient is fixed there rests on the getter and on the shared selector set. Evidence: eth_getCode and eth_call on the rpc URLs of chain ids 1, 10, 8453, 42161, 4663, 137, 56 and 5042 on 2026-11-23, script controllers.py, results in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work/raw/controllers.json; src/ProtocolFees.sol:44-57; research/network-risk/state/ledger.json criticNotes of cycle 5
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. sync has no lock check (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288), while src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:111 names initialize and updateDynamicLPFee as the only functions that run without an unlock. What can an ordinary account do with that, and which network feature turns it into a gain or a freeze for others. Result: An ordinary account can set the synced currency and the reserves value while the manager is locked, and nothing else. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers a sync(T) from a plain contract outside any unlock succeeded for a stub T that answers balanceOf with 32 bytes. exttload then returned T in the currency slot and the answer in the reserves slot, the lock flag read 0, and sync(address(0)) cleared the currency slot. The tests of the repository expect this (test/Sync.t.sol:36-41, test/PoolManager.t.sol:1001-1008) and the test double declares sync without a modifier (src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:139-148), so only the interface comment disagrees. A lock check would not narrow what an account can reach. Any contract can call unlock, call sync inside its callback and return with every delta at zero (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). On all 21 networks such an unlock closed and the synced currency stayed in place afterwards, with the lock flag and the delta counter back at 0. A later settle with value in the same call then reverted with NonzeroNativeValue, and it passed once the payer called sync(address(0)) first. That effect is finding F-071 and stays as recorded there. The other network features of the task were walked against the two slots. Code that runs between another payer transfer and its settle: the PoolManager makes no call between those two steps, so such code can come only from the token or from the payer own router. It would not need sync or the missing lock check, because settle and settleFor are open to every caller while the manager is unlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:300-307). A credit captured that way leaves the payer delta open, and the payer unlock reverts at src/PoolManager.sol:112 unless the payer code ignores the amount that settle returns. This is the same on Ethereum. A failed frame: on all 21 networks an unlock whose callback reverted left no lock flag and no delta behind, since the next unlock in the same call opened and closed normally. Transient storage across transactions and inside protocol level batches (assumption A1) was read from client sources by the units of cycle 3 and was not repeated here. Evidence: eth_call with state overrides on the 21 rpc URLs of research/network-risk/state/networks.json on 2026-11-23 at the latest block of each endpoint (near Ethereum block 26,477,978, Celo 83,537,894, Polygon 97,822,132, Arc 32,737,892 and Tempo 50,432,381, the others as listed in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work/raw/tests_<chainId>.json), scripts tests.py and stale.py, results raw/tests_<chainId>.json and raw/stale.json in research/network-risk/cycles/006/core-code-loose-guards.work; src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, 279-288, 300-307, 349-365; test/Sync.t.sol:36-41; src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol:139-148
- Celo, Arc, Polygon, cycle 6. A sync of a native face made before an unlock on Celo, Arc and Polygon, where an ERC-20 address measures the native balance: can one payment be credited under address(0) and under the face, and what does a native payout do while the face is synced. Result: No double credit on any of the three. One eth_call per network ran the walk on the deployed PoolManager at blocks 83,538,264 (Celo), 32,738,581 (Arc) and 97,822,371 (Polygon), with a funded stub as the ordinary account. With the face synced before the unlock, settle with 1000 wei reverted with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356). After a zero value settle cleared the slot, settle with 1000 wei credited 1000 under address(0). A new sync of the face stored the higher balance and the next settle paid 0, so the face delta stayed 0 and the native delta 1000. On Celo a transfer of 1000 through the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 was credited as 1000 under the face id, and take under that id paid 1000 wei of CELO to the recipient. On Arc one unit sent through 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 was credited as 1 under the face id, and take under that id paid 10^12 wei. On Polygon the transfer through 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010 failed and take under that id reverted, so that id can be neither paid in nor paid out. On all three the native balance of the PoolManager ended at its starting value and every delta read 0. A native take while the face is synced made the next settle revert with a Panic on the checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:360), which costs the settler and nobody else. An account whose EIP-7702 designator names 0x1010 on Polygon also reports the native balance of the PoolManager, as does any contract that returns the balance of its argument (src/test/NativeERC20.sol:46-48 models one). Such a face gives a credit only for value that arrives while it is synced, and its transfer function cannot move native funds of the PoolManager. - all 21 networks, cycle 6. A take of a currency address without code succeeds because the transfer accepts empty return data (src/types/Currency.sol:64-74), while src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:174 says take reverts if the amount is not available. What can an ordinary account do with that, and can a pool, a claim or a debt exist under such an address. Result: The account can make take report success without any transfer, at its own cost. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers, inside one unlock: take of 5 units of a codeless address returned success, the caller delta slot read minus 5 and the delta counter 1. sync of that address reverted with empty data, because balanceOf is a high level call whose empty answer cannot be decoded (src/types/Currency.sol:94). settle with nothing synced paid 0. mint of 7 units added a debt of 7 and a claim of 7. clear reverted with MustClearExactPositiveDelta. A separate unlock that only took 5 units reverted with CurrencyNotSettled, and one that took amount 0 closed, on all 21 networks. The ecrecover address 0x01 gave the same answers as the codeless address. For the identity precompile 0x04 take reverted and sync stored a constant, so the next settle paid 0. Under a codeless id a positive delta could come only from settle, from burn, from a pool or from a hook delta. settle is closed because sync reverts. burn needs a claim, and a claim needs a positive delta to pay for the mint. Pool amounts are rounded against the caller (an add owes the amount rounded up and a removal returns it rounded down, src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:261-288 and src/libraries/Pool.sol:206-237) and a hook delta is subtracted from the caller delta (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:230, 242 and 312), so the deltas of all accounts in that currency sum to zero or less. No claim and no debt therefore exists under a codeless id. A pool that names it can be initialized (src/PoolManager.sol:117-142) and can hold only positions that need the other currency alone. The only party that loses from the silent take is the caller that asked for it. A holder of a real credit could lose it this way only if the code of a token disappeared after deposits, which needs a token built for that, for example an account whose owner clears its EIP-7702 delegation. That is the pool creator class of F-013. What such an account exposes: any caller can borrow its whole native and token balance for the length of one unlock and must return it, a caller can book as its own payment any balance rise it can trigger at the account between sync and settle, and anyone can write claim and operator entries into the storage of the account. owner and protocolFeeController read zero there, initialize, swap, modifyLiquidity and donate revert, and no protocol fee can accrue, so collectProtocolFees has nothing to pay. Caller identities that a network creates, against the functions that trust msg.sender without a lock or a role: unlock, sync, the ERC-6909 functions, and the controller check, which the zero address passes on 13 networks. The zero address holds no code on any of the 21 networks, so no contract code and no delegation can act from it. Its nonce is nonzero on nine OP Stack networks (10 on OP Mainnet, Zora and World Chain, 8 on Base, 7 on Unichain, Ink and Soneium, 5 on Celo, 2 on X Layer) and zero on the other twelve. On seven of the nine (Unichain, Zora, World Chain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer) protocolFeeController is the zero address. This unit did not trace which transactions raised the nonce. The open leads L-100 and L-129 ask that for upgrade deposits, and the nonce values belong with them. Arc: the CallFrom precompile lets two helper contracts name the sender of a child call. Both helpers pass their own msg.sender (Memo.sol line 43, Multicall3From.sol lines 43, 58, 81 and 161), and the client rejects a named sender that is neither the calling helper nor the transaction signer (crates/evm/src/evm.rs lines 946 to 955) and rejects every scheme other than CALL (lines 895 to 903). A contract that runs in the middle of another account transaction therefore cannot reach unlock or the ERC-6909 functions as that account. Inside one unlock: settleFor without payment succeeds, clear of 1 with a zero delta reverts with 0xbda73abf, mint, take and burn of 2^127 revert with 0x93dafdf1 (SafeCastOverflow), a take of amount 0 in the codeless currency succeeds, sync of the codeless currency reverts without data, and a nested unlock reverts with 0x5090d6c6. - all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statements that stand against assumption A1 (src/PoolManager.sol:112, 113, 305, 310): can an ordinary account use them on any of the 21 networks. Result: No path in the text. Line 112 reads the transient counter that every _accountDelta call maintains (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378) and line 113 writes the lock slot; both hold for a caller as long as transient storage lives for exactly the transaction and rolls back with a reverted frame. settleFor and clear carry the same modifier as take and settle, so a locked manager rejects them. The feature that would break these lines is a transaction boundary inside or across user calls (protocol batches, system calls, nested runs with an empty transient map), which is the per network question of assumption A1 that earlier cycles answered from client source and simulation. The reading adds nothing that depends on a network. The cycle 3 critic probe showed on all 21 RPC nodes that these slots are scoped by address and that a second transaction reads zero where simulation is offered. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:96-99, 104-114, 305, 310; research/network-risk/state/ledger.json criticNotes cycle 3
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statements that stand against assumption A2 (src/PoolManager.sol:360, 361, 364): a balance that falls between sync and settle, a balance rise credited twice, and a balance reading of 2^127 or more. Result: As written, a fall makes the checked subtraction revert, the reset after settle means a rise is credited once, and a rise of 2^127 or more reverts in toInt128. An ordinary account can still book a rise that a third party or the token itself causes between its own sync and settle, which is the class of F-041 and its variants and needs no unpinned line. I found no way to use these three statements beyond that class. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:349-365
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statements that stand against assumptions A4 and A7 (src/types/Currency.sol:48, 64-74, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152, 166): a currency or hook address without code or at a precompile, and the gas forwarded to a native recipient. Result: A take of a currency whose address returns success and no data debits the caller and moves nothing, so the caller loses and no one else does; a credit in such an id needs sync, which reverts when balanceOf returns no data (confirmed on all 21 deployed contracts in the probe above for an address without code). A hook answer shorter than 32 bytes is rejected. A native payout forwards all gas to the recipient, which is lever P1 of ASSUMPTIONS.md and was swept per network in earlier cycles (F-021, F-047, F-048, F-049). These lines give an ordinary account no way to take or lock funds of others in the text as written. Evidence: src/types/Currency.sol:44-87, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-168
- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Unpinned statement that stands against assumption A8 (src/PoolManager.sol:335): burn takes claims from a named account and credits msg.sender. Result: burn calls _burnFrom, which requires msg.sender to be the holder, an operator of the holder, or to have an allowance of at least the amount for that id (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). The credit goes to msg.sender, so the only question a network can change is who msg.sender is. A caller identity that the chain forges (aliased cross domain senders, system callers) would still need the holder's approval for that identity. On all 21 deployed contracts a burn of another address's claims by an unapproved caller gave no credit. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:332-336, src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22

Ethereum, 2 rows: an account with delegated code calls unlock itself, syncs sDAI 0x83f20f44975d03b1b09e64809b757c47f942beea, deposits its own DAI into sDAI with the PoolManager as receiver (selector 0x6e553f65), settles 8,438.31 sDAI and takes it out again (transaction 0x0967eff055f702371ab99ad27bb9db815ca4c24cec84d7cd16a12ed96bcc94e4). The receipt holds a Deposit log of sDAI for the PoolManager and no Transfer log to it, and the caller paid the DAI. Base, 6 rows: three reflection tokens (0xbc3dabf2f77e58859c6a2ba9bf5393a0d08ff363, 0x74f84a0add717a6c405b2c8c0b82d94b514e113e, 0x4e27de65c2124a93d9a9446156893fe38914f057) credit the payer 0.0007 to 0.7 percent more than the Transfer log, because the PoolManager balance earns its holder share during the incoming transfer, and one token differs by one unit. Lending receipt tokens credit one unit, or the interest of the block, more than the log on Ethereum (5 rows), OP Mainnet (3), Arbitrum One (3), Robinhood Chain (1) and Polygon (1), and on Avalanche one row pays out one unit more than came in. BNB Smart Chain, 4 rows: stHYPER 0x6e9804a08092d8ba4e69dacf422df12459f2599e logs 18.06 units for a transfer that raises balanceOf by 31.97, so its logs and its balances use different units, and two other tokens credit a few units or a holder share of 2.6 percent above the log. On Polygon 248 open rows and 13 spoof rows carry the address 0xe0aea583266584dafbb3f9c3211d5588c73fea8d: they are payouts of the old EURe id 0x18ec0a6e18e5bc3784fdd3a3634b31245ab704f6, which logs at the new address (F-075). In 20 of 25 sampled rows the Swap amount of the old id equals the logged outflow. The other five hold liquidity events of pools of the old id, which I did not reconcile. Evidence: https://mainnet.gateway.tenderly.co
- BNB Smart Chain, cycle 6. BNB Smart Chain rows of tokens that are in no pool although the reported PoolManager balance fell: 21 rows over 13 contracts in the 3 day census. Result: All 13 are dividend trackers of pooled tokens (names such as ETHBack_Dividend_Tracker and DIVIDEND_TRACKER). A tracker repeats the balance that each holder has in the main token and logs a Transfer when it changes, so its figure for the PoolManager falls when a pool pays the main token out. None is a currency of a pool. A transfer of one unit from the PoolManager reverts on each of them, for 11 with the text No transfers allowed, so a pool created with a tracker as currency could be credited through sync and settle and never paid out, as with the mirror tokens of F-008 and F-050. The PoolManager is not excluded from dividends on the trackers that answer excludedFromDividends. The reward tokens are USDT, BUSD, DOGE, ASTER, BNCB and DogeZilla. withdrawableDividendOf(PoolManager) is zero on 10 trackers and dust on the others today. Rewards that a tracker pays to the PoolManager are not recorded by any pool. A lead asks how much has been paid and whether a public claim lets a caller book it. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/006/theme-currency-lists.work/raw/bnb_trackers.json

- Ethereum, Base, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Robinhood Chain, cycle 6. Single token bonding curve hooks with flags beforeInitialize, beforeAddLiquidity, beforeSwap, beforeSwapReturnDelta that hold native ETH, BNB or AVAX (SatoHook 0x0000f07d2b5f1ddf3244b8780f972f306efd2888 with 981.27 ETH, SurtHook, Sat1Hook, VitaHook, SatopegHook on Ethereum, BloomHook, HookTemplate, J3sseHook on Base, three SatoHook copies and AizoHook on BNB Smart Chain, one on Avalanche, NakamotoHook with 25.89 ETH on Robinhood Chain): they accept a second pool. Can it reach the reserve?. Result: No. SatoHook source lines 224 to 231: beforeInitialize requires currency0 native, currency1 the hook's own token, fee 3000 and this hook, so a second pool can differ in tick spacing only. beforeSwap (253 to 272) checks the two currencies again and trades against one curve state (ethCum, totalMintedFair), so every pool of the hook is the same market for the same token. beforeAddLiquidity always reverts. The probe confirms it for the family: foreign pairs revert with InvalidPool and only the own pair with another tick spacing is accepted. For the hooks other than SatoHook I relied on the probe and on the matching error selectors, without reading each source. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x0000f07d2b5f1ddf3244b8780f972f306efd2888
- Ethereum, Arc, cycle 6. RobinVistaHook 0xc2988a37d611779ad34b561231ee33603d15a0cc on Ethereum (160 pools, claims of 9.24 ETH plus PEPE, UNI, ONDO and others, about 18,100 USD) keeps accrued and banked fees per launch token, and poolIdOf[launchToken] is overwritten on every registerPool. Can an account register a second pool of a token with another base currency and withdraw in it? LongHook 0xfb6369c30573f9af1b88314c732fca944a34e0cc on Arc has the same mappings. Result: Not through the deployed factory. The ledger has the Klik shape: fees are added to accrued[launchToken] in the base token of the swapping pool and withdrawn in the base token of the pool that poolIdOf[launchToken] points at (hook lines 178 to 199, 296 to 366). registerPool and beforeInitialize accept allowed factories only, and one FactorySet log exists, for RobinVistaFactory 0x5407f136d0ddd6e6edcf5d2720ee7e26eeb9ac9a. Its launchToken (lines 309 to 419) deploys a new clone token for every launch and takes the base token from an owner curated registry, so each launch token has one pool and one base token. The fault would open if the owner allowed a factory that registers a pool for an existing token. For LongHook I read the mappings and the factory gate only, and did not read its factory. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x5407f136d0ddd6e6edcf5d2720ee7e26eeb9ac9a
- Ethereum, cycle 6. Result: OndexHook stores treasury, creator, holder and liquidity amounts in ledger[PoolId] (lines 100 to 108) and accepts initialize from its factory only (258 to 263). LaunchHook stores launches per pool id, its FeeEscrow is claimable[recipient][currency], and beforeInitialize requires the hook itself as sender. LaunchpadHook stores curves per pool id and creatorEthOwed per coin, all 211 pools pair with native ETH, and beforeInitialize requires a curve already registered for the pool id. EthCreatorFeeHookV3 stores its configuration per pool id and accepts the registrar of that configuration only. None of them pays from a ledger that omits both the pool id and the currency. - Ethereum, cycle 6. TurbineHook 0x1be2e33d8f468c09c1aa9e53d54e400470b2a088 (three pools, claims of 14,720 USDC and 0.4 WETH): beforeInitialize registers any currency pair with tick spacing 1 from any caller, and beforeSwap mints input claims and burns output claims. Can a pool opened by a stranger burn the claims of the real pools?. Result: No. beforeSwap, mint and burn carry the routerOnly modifier (lines 222 to 280 and 370 to 424), so only swaps sent by the Turbine router reach the claim moves, with the output amount supplied by that router. The hook keeps reserve0 and reserve1 per pool id and updates them with checked arithmetic, and a source comment at line 246 states that the ERC-6909 balance cannot be used because it aggregates all pools of the hook. A new pool starts with zero reserves, so a swap out of it reverts on the subtraction. The router itself was not read. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x1be2e33d8f468c09c1aa9e53d54e400470b2a088
- Robinhood Chain, Arc, X Layer, Base, cycle 6. Launch pad hooks named in L-395 that have verified source: CashCatHook and CashCatHookV2, PonsV2MemeHook, the proxy 0x4eb1976978756bd56802d8162f2271844924e0cc and FablesRamp on Robinhood Chain, MinaraFeeHook, WonkHook and LaunchHook on Arc, TaxLaunchHook on X Layer and Base. Is the ledger that decides a payout stored under the pool id, a token or a currency, and who may initialize?. Result: All are stored under the pool id or under the currency that is paid. CashCatHookV2: pending and tab per pool id, platformTab per currency, initialize from the factory only and currency0 must equal the configured quote (line 273). CashCatHook: per pool id, native quote only. PonsV2MemeHook: pendingFees, pendingCreatorTax and pendingBuyback per pool id and currency, factory only. 0x4eb19769 is an ERC-1967 proxy of LunchTaxHookPair: accruedQuote per pool id, owed per recipient and quote token, launcher only. FablesRamp: range ledgers per pool, distributorOwed and claimFeeOwed per currency, initialize needs a fee cap configured for the pool id. MinaraFeeHook: creatorAccrued per pool id, platformAccrued per currency, launcher only with an allowed quote. WonkHook: per pool id and currency, initialize needs a registered launch. TaxLaunchHook: configuration and fee slots per pool id, escrow per recipient and currency, factory only. The factories were not read, so whether a launcher may choose the quote currency is answered only where the hook checks it (CashCatHookV2, MinaraFeeHook). ZoraV4CoinHook 0x0469a4bd3724dc86c9542f4694c976da13c450c0 on Base holds nothing in the currencies checked and rejects initialize. - Ethereum, Arbitrum One, BNB Smart Chain, Monad, cycle 6. UniswapV4KEMHook 0x4440854b2d02c57a0dc5c58b7a884562d875c0c4 (107 pools on Ethereum, claims of about 4,700 USD in many currencies, also on Arbitrum One and BNB Smart Chain, same code on Monad at 0x4445520306c9c70952bdfec28f3989f53d9f80c4) and the unverified 0x83863f772f93e2a209dab0af924ca3d6764a40c4 (about 2,000 USD of claims on BNB Smart Chain, 618 USD on Arbitrum One) have no initialize flag and no ledger at all. Can a foreign pool spend the claims?. Result: No path found. The hooks have no state mapping, and the claims are surplus kept for the hook operator, so there is no balance owed to a particular pool. For a foreign pool beforeSwap reverts with 0x3b99b53d (0x87fa6e44 on the unverified one) because the swap carries no signed quote, and afterSwap alone reverts with Panic(0x12). The claim withdrawal function was not read. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/1/0x4440854b2d02c57a0dc5c58b7a884562d875c0c4
- Polygon, cycle 6. PolHook 0xa33c9bcd5cada0636f19350d7461003c38814088 and 0xb721b4f9771ed66f85c0ffbf9504f1eaab154088 on Polygon have the same shape as the Arbitrum route hooks: beforeSwap takes the PoolKey input currency and trades hardcoded DAI and USDT on a Curve pool from the hook balance (source lines 53 to 115). They hold 3.0 DAI each and 2.24 USDT. Can a foreign pool empty them?. Result: Not today. In the Quoter test inside an unlock the hook takes the foreign currency and Curve pulls 2.9994 DAI from the hook, and then exchange_underlying reverts because the Aave V2 lending pool 0x8dff5e27ea6b7ac08ebfdf9eb090f32ee9a30fcf rejects the deposit with error string "3". The same revert hits the hooks' own DAI and USDT pool, so the hooks are out of service. The balances are about 3 USD each. beforeSwap in this source has no caller check either. If the Aave reserve accepts deposits again the path opens. Evidence: https://sourcify.dev/server/v2/contract/137/0xa33c9bcd5cada0636f19350d7461003c38814088
- Unichain, Arbitrum One, cycle 6. Hooks that call PoolManager.take or PoolManager.swap with hardcoded currencies inside beforeSwap for any pool, and hold nothing: Unichain proxy 0xad78e0a3b5a552813feb5eb8ecbe842f7b5e9088 (takes native ETH and swaps on a real pool for a foreign PoolKey) and the exact output branch of CamelotHook on Arbitrum One. Can this move PoolManager funds to the swapper?. Result: No. take debits the hook in the currency it names (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297) and the delta it returns is credited in the currencies of the foreign PoolKey (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:299-311), so the hook is left with a debt in the real currency that nobody settles and unlock reverts with CurrencyNotSettled (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114). The Quoter shows a result only because it reverts before that check. A loss needs a hook that owns claims or balances, as in the two findings. Evidence: src/PoolManager.sol:104
- Arbitrum One, cycle 6. Unverified hook 0x6bc99d37114ae54b782c7694368ed5430e9c0ac8 on Arbitrum One (1001 USDC and 1001 USDT on the hook, two pools, no initialize flag): afterSwap does not look at the PoolKey. For any pool it reads prices from 0x451d7e6f and calls PositionManager.modifyLiquiditiesWithoutUnlock on its own position 0x2afe. Result: No loss shown. In the Quoter test for five foreign PoolKeys the third modifyLiquiditiesWithoutUnlock call reverts and afterSwap fails with a wrapped error, so a foreign pool cannot be swapped at all. The rebalance uses the oracle price and the hook's own position, and anyone can trigger the same code by swapping in the real pool. Whether a foreign swap can succeed in another state and move the position at a price the attacker sets was not established and is listed as a lead. Evidence: https://arbitrum.drpc.org

## Reading of the source (theme-token-triggers)

- all 21 networks, cycle 6. Step 1. Which pooled tokens with a market price are worth more than 1,000 USD at each PoolManager today. Method: currency lists of cycle 4, live balanceOf(PoolManager), prices from coins.llama.fi (cycle 5 price files for 18 networks; this cycle priced every currency with a balance on Robinhood Chain, Elysium and Arc, 738,773, 129,491 and 261,204 addresses). Result: 2151 tokens on 19 networks, 1080 of them above 10,000 USD: Ethereum 845 (427 above 10,000 USD); Optimism 29 (9 above 10,000 USD); Base 323 (200 above 10,000 USD); Unichain 18 (12 above 10,000 USD); Zora 0 (0 above 10,000 USD); Worldchain 12 (9 above 10,000 USD); Ink 19 (15 above 10,000 USD); Soneium 6 (2 above 10,000 USD); Celo 5 (3 above 10,000 USD); X Layer 14 (7 above 10,000 USD); Arbitrum One 85 (48 above 10,000 USD); Robinhood Chain 353 (183 above 10,000 USD); Elysium 18 (12 above 10,000 USD); Polygon 70 (36 above 10,000 USD); BNB Smart Chain 250 (67 above 10,000 USD); Avalanche 22 (8 above 10,000 USD); Monad 34 (22 above 10,000 USD); MegaETH 2 (1 above 10,000 USD); Tempo 5 (4 above 10,000 USD); Arc 41 (15 above 10,000 USD); HyperEVM 0 (0 above 10,000 USD). Zora and HyperEVM have no priced token above the threshold (2 and 11 priced currencies, all below 1,000 USD). The lists are complete where cycle 4 read every Initialize log (Ethereum, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Arc and the other networks with an init census). They are incomplete on Base, BNB Smart Chain and X Layer, where the cycle 4 list holds only currencies that moved in its window, and on World Chain, where it comes from an explorer page. A census of Base Initialize logs started in this cycle counted 2,418,681 currencies in the first 10,000,000 blocks after deployment against 9,116 on the list, and was stopped for size. Two values are price artefacts and were kept as targets: PORT3 on Ethereum and vUSDT on BNB Smart Chain, whose balanceOf returns more than one word. Token lists with values are in the discover files. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/006/theme-token-triggers.work/raw/stats.json
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Monad, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc, cycle 6. Step 2. For each of the 2151 tokens: every selector of the token, of its implementation and of the contracts that balanceOf(PoolManager) touches (eth_createAccessList, 1442 related contracts) was called from an ordinary account with the PoolManager as address argument. Named functions got arguments by type; the 14775 selectors without a known name got eight fixed calldata shapes. Each trial ran in eth_call with a measuring stub at the PoolManager address and was repeated with the block time moved by 8 hours, 91 days and 400 days. Mode A: the stub hands one third of the balance to the account first. Mode B: the PoolManager sends nothing and the account holds a balance written by state override into the token's balance slot. Mode C: as B without a balance, for tokens whose slot was not found. Measured: balanceOf(PoolManager) before and after, the account's balance, and whether a transfer of the full balance leaves the PoolManager. Result: Mode A 2318914 trials, 140312 calls accepted by the token. Mode B 2279949 trials on 2019 tokens, 133089 accepted. Mode C 38965 trials on 132 tokens. Batches that failed for lack of gas were rerun with eight trials per call and none is left open. One priced token ended a trial with a higher reported balance and a refused full transfer: QANX 0xaaa7a10a8ee237ea61e8ac46c50a8db8bcc1baaa on Ethereum through transferLocked, at every block time. That is finding F-078 and nothing new (21,210,277.64 units at the PoolManager, 205,708 USD at the coins.llama.fi figure that F-078 already calls unreliable). No trial lowered balanceOf(PoolManager) of a priced token, at any of the four times. Every other accepted call that raised the balance took the same amount from the caller and left the full balance transferable (transfer, transferAndCall, multiTransfer, batchTransfer, transferShares and equals), or differed by one or two base units of share rounding. The full list of functions through which a caller's tokens reached the PoolManager is transfer, transferFrom, transferAndCall, transferWithMemo, multiTransfer, batchTransfer, push, move, transferShares, bridgeTransfer, bridgeTransferFrom, transferMultiple, transferForMultiAddresses, transferWithReference, transferFromWithReference, multisend and bulkTransfer. None is a grant, a lock or a deposit for another account, so no priced token offers the grant and revoke sequence of F-079, and no selector without a name raised the balance. One mode B result is an artefact: claimRewardsAndStake on stkAAVE paid the account's own rewards, which exist only because of the overridden balance, to the PoolManager. Control: DeadToken on Base (F-085) is not detected in mode A, because the hand-out by the PoolManager resets its idle timer, and is detected in mode B at 91 and 400 days (claimIdleTokens lowers the balance to 0 and the account gains half). Limits: the trials measure the token's own balance only, so a public call that pays a second asset to the PoolManager is not seen; arguments such as Merkle proofs and signatures are not satisfied; on Monad no endpoint accepted a block override, so Monad was tested at the current time only. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/006/theme-token-triggers.work/sweep.py, raw/sweep_<chain>.json.gz, raw/sweepB_<chain>.json.gz, raw/sweepC_<chain>.json.gz
- Ethereum, Optimism, Base, Unichain, Worldchain, Ink, Soneium, Celo, X Layer, Arbitrum One, Robinhood Chain, Elysium, Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, MegaETH, Tempo, Arc, cycle 6. Does the passage of time alone change the PoolManager balance of a target token or stop it from sending the full balance (expiry, demurrage, cooldown, scheduled rebase)? One block was pinned per network and the trial without any call was run at 0, 8 hours, 91 days and 400 days, with and without a hand-out. Result: Six tokens change, all Aave receipt tokens whose balance grows with interest: aEthLINK, aEthWETH, aEthUSDC and aEthUSDT on Ethereum, aArbUSDT on Arbitrum One and aBasWETH on Base (each between 1,500 and 5,800 USD). No token lost balance with time and no full balance transfer turned from accepted to refused at any of the shifted times. Monad could not be tested for lack of a block override. Evidence: research/network-risk/cycles/006/theme-token-triggers.work/timeonly.py, raw/timeonly_<chain>.json.gz
- Base, Tempo, cycle 6. Precompile tokens have no selector table in code: 35 B20 tokens on Base (OUSD with 5.3 million USD, the tokenized stocks with suffix c, cbZEC, cbHYPE) and the 5 TIP-20 tokens on Tempo. The function lists were taken from the published interfaces and run through the same trials. Result: Base B20: 30 state changing functions of IB20, IB20Asset and IERC8056; 3,920 trials per mode; an ordinary account gets transfer, transferWithMemo and approve accepted and nothing else. mint, burnBlocked, seizeWithMemo, pause, updatePolicy and the multiplier setters need roles, and the interface states that balanceOf stays in raw units while the multiplier scales the UI view only. Tempo TIP-20: 29 functions, 620 trials per mode, the accepted calls are transfers, approve and calls that act on the caller. burnBlocked and burnAt need roles, and rewards are claimed by the holder for itself. Issuer powers over these tokens are in F-027 and the Tempo findings of earlier cycles. All 310 bids were read at Ethereum block 26,478,229: none has the PoolManager as owner, 10 are not exited and 1 is exited with 8.33 FOLD unclaimed, all owned by other addresses. lockCount(PoolManager), queuedLockCount(PoolManager) and lockedBalanceOf(PoolManager) are 0 and transferableBalanceOf equals balanceOf. The remaining ways to place a lock (linkClaim, mintAllocations) need LOCK_MANAGER_ROLE or MINTER_ROLE, and minting is closed since tge. ## Reading of the source (audit-walk-a)

- all 21 networks, cycle 7. OpenZeppelin audit, C-01: an ERC-20 representation of the native currency lets one payment be credited twice, once as msg.value under address(0) and once as a balance increase under the token, which drains native pools (worked case Celo, with Polygon as a network where deltas can be inflated). Result: Closed in the source. Hazard in one sentence: sync the token face, pay with settle and value, then settle the face for the same inflow. Closing statements: a settle with value reverts while any token is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356); a native credit is taken from msg.value only when no currency is synced (353-354); every write of a nonzero synced currency also writes the reserves (285-286, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:27-32), so a face synced after a native payment starts from the higher balance; a token settle clears the slot (361); the contract has no receive or fallback function and only settle and settleFor are payable (300-307). The report says the fix makes the next settle after a sync settle that currency or revert. The source is looser in one way: sync(address(0)) clears the slot without a settle (283, documented at src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:165-171). I walked the orders that this allows and each inflow is still credited under one id only, because the stale reserves are overwritten by the next token sync. Reliance: A1 (the synced currency lives in transient storage for one transaction and is rolled back on revert), A2 and A3 (native value reaches the PoolManager through settle, and anything forced in is credited once under one id). Per network: an address that reports the PoolManager's native balance exists on Celo (CELO token, transfer works), Arc (0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000, six decimals, transfer works), Polygon (0x1010, transfer of 1 without value returned false), Optimism and Zora (LegacyERC20ETH, transfer disabled). My query found no such answer from these candidates on the other 16 networks, and the ledger holds a face search for each of them. On all 21 deployed PoolManagers my walk with a stub token that returns the native balance of its argument gave: sync while locked succeeded, settle with 1000 wei reverted with NonzeroNativeValue, a zero value settle paid 0 and cleared the slot, settle with 1000 wei then credited 1000, a new sync and settle of the face paid 0, and a native take of 1000 closed the unlock. The real faces on Celo, Polygon, Arc, Optimism and Zora gave the same seven answers. The walk shows the contracts deployed today. The checkout was not compiled. Evidence: docs/security/audits/OpenZeppelin_audit_core.pdf pages 10-11; src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 300-307, 349-365; src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32; eth_call with state overrides on the 21 rpc URLs of state/networks.json on 2026-11-23 (scripts walk.py and faces.py, results raw/walk.json and raw/faces.json in cycles/007/core-code-audit-walk-a.work); cleared items of core-code-accounting (cycle 1), core-code-invariants-settlement (cycle 2) and core-code-loose-guards (cycle 6)

OpenZeppelin audit, security model and trust assumptions (page 9): core has no slippage protection, non-standard and malicious tokens are not supported, malicious hooks can take from users of their pool, and anyone can create a pool with any token. Result: These are stated limits and nothing in src closes them. What src provides is separation: pool state is stored per pool id (src/PoolManager.sol:93), deltas per caller and currency (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41), hook deltas are booked to the hook address in the two currencies of its pool (PoolManager.sol:181, 224, 381-384). Reliance: A2 and A4 for tokens, A7 for hooks. The ledger records where these fail per network (rebasing and reward tokens F-012, F-041, F-066, F-067, F-091, tokens that move or burn the PoolManager balance F-085, F-086, F-090, F-099, issuer controls F-057, F-080). - all 21 networks, cycle 7. OpenZeppelin audit, M-01: assembly blocks marked memory-safe wrote past the scratch space or over the free memory pointer (hook return data, the TickMisaligned error, two argument custom errors, the ERC-20 transfer call). Result: Closed. The hook return data is copied to memory at the free memory pointer, which is then advanced by the padded length (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:140-149). TickMisaligned and the two argument revert helpers build their data at the free memory pointer and revert at once (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:57-63, src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:49-79, 83-118). The single argument helpers write 36 bytes into the 64 byte scratch space (CustomRevert.sol:14-46). The ERC-20 transfer writes its 68 bytes of calldata at the free memory pointer, reads the answer into the first scratch word and zeroes the three words it used (src/types/Currency.sol:55-80). Reliance: A10 only, that MSTORE, MLOAD, RETURNDATACOPY and CALL behave as on Ethereum, which cycle 1 tested on every network. - all 21 networks, cycle 7. Trail of Bits audit, finding 1: a strict equality in the 100 percent fee check would let a swap fee above 100 percent pass. Result: Closed. The check is swapFee >= SwapMath.MAX_SWAP_FEE and rejects exact output swaps (src/libraries/Pool.sol:311-316). I also checked that the fee cannot exceed the maximum at all: a static fee is validated at initialize (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:51-56, src/PoolManager.sol:128), a dynamic fee at updateDynamicLPFee (PoolManager.sol:343), an override at Pool.sol:303-305, each against 1,000,000, the protocol fee against 1000 per direction (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32), and the combined fee is protocolFee + lpFee - floor(protocolFee * lpFee / 1,000,000) (lines 38-46). A Python run over every protocol fee from 0 to 1000 and 3,200 LP fees each, the top 1,000 values included, gave a maximum of exactly 1,000,000 and never less than the protocol fee, which also keeps the unchecked subtraction at Pool.sol:395 from wrapping. The closing statement uses no property of the chain, so it holds on all 21 networks alike.
